We have validated the efficacy of this strategy through both simulation and experimental evaluations, demonstrating its applicability and performance in dense environments.

The Seidel matrix A_G of a graph G is defined as an n by n matrix with elements from the set {0, 1}, where n represents the number of distinct vertex pairs in G. In this particular study, we examine the Seidel matrix for chain graphs, which have a specific ordering pattern. Our findings indicate that the Seidel matrix of a chain graph has a range that includes all possible 2 by 2 matrices with entries from the set {0, 1}, where this matrix's spectral radius is less than or equal to 1. Moreover, the natural matrix product of two Seidel matrices at a chain graph results in another Seidel matrix corresponding to a modified chain graph, where this new graph's number of vertices is equivalent to the square of the original. Additionally, we have shown that the Seidel matrix of a chain graph is diagonalizable and its eigenvalues are relatively prime. Our analysis further reveals that the characteristic polynomial of the Seidel matrix is either divisible by (x+1)(x+1)^m or has no common factors of x and 1+x, where m represents the length of the chain graph's given ordering.

The literature on stochastic differential equations driven by Brownian motion has extensively addressed optimal control problems in response to linear constraints and reference trajectories. However, research is limited regarding the mean-field optimization of such equations, which are influenced by a fractional Brownian motion. This study aims to fill this knowledge gap, developing a novel framework for mean-field optimal control problems governed by stochastic differential equations driven by a fractional Brownian motion. Utilizing the fractional Yamada-Watsontype approach, we establish the existence and uniqueness of the desired path. Furthermore, we formulate the maximum principle under stochastic reference trajectories, and illustrate the main results through a numerical example.

We examine finite-band elliptic energies associated with the non-self-adjoint Dirac operator, represented by a finite-band Toeplitz operator with Hermitian quasicomponential generating function. These energies demonstrate a connection to the characteristic polynomial of a symmetric Toeplitz operator. Additionally, in the case of a constant symbol, our findings align with those from existing literature on non-self-adjoint Dirac operator. Furthermore, this investigation yields a recursive relationship for the characteristic polynomial, allowing us to derive explicit or implicit expressions for the recursive structure of the band widths and the characteristic polynomials themselves. Notably, this analysis also identifies a connection to the Frechet smoothness of non-self-adjoint Dirac operator's spectral shift function.

The integration of Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) with vehicular ad-hoc networks (VANETs) has revolutionized transportation systems by providing safety-critical applications and enhanced services to vehicle users. To overcome coverage limitations and maximize connectivity, this dissertation proposes and evaluates a dual-tier network architecture, combining vehicle relays and road-side units. Specifically, an intersection-based vehicular relay architecture is designed to utilize vehicles as all-inclusive nodes, leveraging their computing capabilities and connectivity. A two-tier network model is implemented using a metropolitan-scale scenario, showcasing the efficacy of vehicle relays in augmenting network coverage and capacity. Moreover, an extensive performance assessment is performed to identify key factors influencing the performance of this next-generation vehicular network design.

Wikipedia's vast potential for learning and research is threatened by the growing problem of low-quality content. Despite Wikipedia's established system for labeling article issues via "tags," editors struggle to keep up with the growing burden. The main obstacle is identifying which articles require improvement, given the vast number of articles and limited editing capacity. Our study explores the possibility of utilizing automatic tagging by identifying patterns in contributor behavior that predict article quality. We assessed the efficacy of various tagging systems, featuring different feature sets, and discovered that incorporating metadata from edit history and user activities yields better results. The top-performing system achieved a precision of 0.041, recall of 0.041, and F1 score of 0.081 when compared to human editors, who achieved a precision of 0.070, recall of 0.070, and F1 score of 0.080. Although the current approach faces limitations, such as relying on existing tags to train the model, our study provides a framework for future improvements, including self-improvement through iterative editing.

One major issue with relying on user input in decision-based black-box models is that they can't utilize valuable unlabelled data to refine their decision-making capabilities. This paper proposes an approach to resolve this limitation by equipping decision-based black-box models with the ability to draw upon unlabelled data, allowing them to gain improved performance without requiring annotated training. To achieve this, we design a novel knowledge transfer framework that facilitates a trained model known as the 'teacher' to provide guidance to an untrained model known as the'student'. This transfer framework utilizes the teacher to classify unlabelled samples, which are then used as labelled examples to educate the student. As a result, the student can attain superior decision-making performance without requiring annotated training. Experimental outcomes reveal that this knowledge transfer framework offers results on par with high-quality labelled training data, without needing any labelled examples. This research presents the first known solution to get decision-based black-box models to draw upon unlabelled data, offering numerous practical benefits. Moreover, the proposed knowledge transfer framework demonstrates the ability to transfer its capabilities to future scenarios, showcasing a key advantage over existing knowledge transfer methods.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_L$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_L$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb. The branching fractions for these decays are calculated as follows: The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (4.3±0.5±0.3±0.3±1.0) ×10^-4, and the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (2.8±1.0±0.3±0.2±0.4 ±0.9 ±0.5) ×10^-4, with the given uncertainties stemming from various sources.

We've developed a precise method for performing geometric T-duality between lattices in the context of twisted tori. Our method accurately transforms the twisted string spectrum, which in turn allows for the reconstruction of original string theories from reduced forms. We demonstrate that our reduced forms exhibit circular orbifold symmetry, where T-duality can be realized through the action of the isometry group. We've also discovered a relationship between our reduced forms and the SL(2,Z) transformation on the worldsheet.

In recent years, research has increased on collaborative learning between humans and machines, but most current studies rely on experts actively contributing to model training. This paper examines the feasibility of improving collaborative learning outcomes without requiring experts to manually provide data for model training. To achieve this, we present a novel approach called co-observation learning, which enables machines to observe and learn from experts' unmarked interactions with students. Utilizing eye-tracking data from teachers, we demonstrate that machines can leverage this information to improve their student correction performance in an online tutoring setting. Furthermore, we investigate various conditions under which machines can utilize data collected from different students and achieve improved outcomes. Our findings indicate that machines trained under the co-observation learning framework can achieve performance comparable to that of humans, highlighting potential applications in scenarios where expert expertise needs to be transmitted to numerous individuals.

This paper proposes a metric and an error correction method for Deterministic Automatic Coding of Permutations (PAC) codes, which are used to correct permutation errors in datasets. The proposed metric calculates the cost of permuting elements in a dataset to match a reference dataset, making it applicable to diverse data types. This work also develops a decoding algorithm to correct single permutation errors, which leverages the code's structure to improve efficiency, particularly for codes with high rates. The proposed approach enables the calculation of coding rates for PAC codes, which is crucial for coding theories involving codes with non-integer rates.

Accurately capturing the complex movements and positions of hands and their interaction with objects in unstructured outdoor environments has long been a challenge for computer vision. In this research, we present a novel, depth-camera-based system that can effectively monitor the trajectory of hands and their interaction with objects in the non-studio outdoor setting. Our system employs a depth sensor and tracks the movements of hands in a sequence of point cloud images captured by the sensor. Leveraging a novel hand representation that thrives in uncertain and dynamic environments, we have developed a method to estimate the movement of hands and correct any errors that may occur. Furthermore, we employ a probabilistic tracking approach to follow the movement of hands and their interaction with objects over time. Our research is the first to successfully document the interaction of hands with objects in a sequence of tracked point clouds. Our approach consists of two critical components: a highly efficient tracking system that associates corresponding points in consecutive cloud images and estimates the movement of hands, and a novel, low-complexity routine that reconstructs the three-dimensional poses of hands and their interaction with objects. In particular, our approach focuses on the reconstruction of object-hand interactions, an aspect that has received scarce attention thus far. In our research, we have developed a probabilistic model to link the reconstruction of point clouds and the trajectory of hands and their interaction with objects. Furthermore, we employ a variational inference method to refine the estimated hand item poses. Our system demonstrated exceptional performance in tracking and reconstructing the

A specific class of infinite transfinite groups, denoted as $t_{\Lambda}^{(n)}(G)$, can be used to classify a type of infinite transfinite group known as $LC$-groups. This classification utilizes a finite group $G$ and a directed set $\Lambda$ with a flag function $f$. By examining the various $t_{\Lambda}^{(n)}(G)$ groups for different choices of $\Lambda$ and $f$, one can determine the required properties for a finite group $G$ to be classified as an $LC$-group. Specifically, this involves showing that, for a finite group $G$, if it satisfies certain conditions related to its indices and subgroups, then an $LC$-subgroup of degree 4 in $G$ will have an interlacing number of 2. This is achieved by proving that, for a finite group $G$, if it satisfies specific conditions related to its indices and subgroups, then an $LC$-subgroup of degree 4 in $G$ will have an interlacing number of 2. This is done by first establishing the criteria for noncrystallographic tail-triangle $LC$-subgroups of grade 4 in a finite group $G$. A robot's efficiency can be significantly enhanced by utilizing information from a depth camera, enabling precise calculation of its end-effector's location and orientation. However, the process of aligning the robot and the depth camera, referred as registration, is a complex task, particularly in cases where the robot's appearance or movement causes variations in the depth sensor's data. In situations where point-cloud data is not labeled, finding correspondence between robot and depth sensor data becomes even more challenging. This paper presents an innovative and efficient two-stage process to estimate correspondences between the two datasets. The initial stage utilizes a depth-based similarity measure to create a correspondence graph, whereas the second stage applies a robust voting algorithm to determine optimal correspondences. Once reliable correspondences are established, the robot's pose can be calculated using a voting-based approach. Our proposed method is capable of handling unmarked data, thereby reducing computational costs associated with labeling. Moreover, its simplicity enables it to operate in real-time, enabling registration during actual robot movements. Our experiments using simulated and real data confirm that our method is highly accurate and efficient.

This study presents a novel method to determine the local interference structure among units treated in the vicinity of a central treated unit. Specifically, we devise a nonparametric test to establish the 1-nearest-neighbor (1NN) interference framework for continuous and binary outcomes. Given that establishing the full interference model is complicated and requires considerable data resources, we propose using a data-driven approach to assess the validity of the 1NN framework and test the specific hypothesis of k-nearest-neighbor (kNN) interference, including the commonly utilized 1NN framework. In applications involving spatial data, we propose refining the kNN interference model by incorporating geographic weights. Empirical evidence from various practical scenarios illustrates the efficacy of our method.

The ongoing UNIONS/CFIS survey is conducting a comprehensive morphological study of $67\,654\,634$ galaxies across the degree-square area in the northern Galactic plane, employing $141\,\mathrm{deg}^2$ of depth. The stochastic approach of weak gravitational lensing technique is utilized to analyze large populations of elliptical galaxies for their average ellipticity, using two-point correlation function as the primary analysis method. The analysis is carried out on a total of $34.4\, \mathrm{deg}^2$ of weak-lensed galaxy data with high signal-to-noise ratio, yielding an estimate of the cosmic shear variance, $\sigma_{\omega(e)}$, of $0.0811\pm 0.0049$, in agreement with the predicted value from the Planck 2015 cosmological parameters. This is the most extensive weak-lensing analysis conducted to date on a morphological survey dataset.

Investigating the behavior of vectors within lattice structures has historically been achieved through analysis, with many notable results obtained by translating the study into the context of diophantine approximation. A notable achievement in this area is the establishment of K-W equidistribution by Elkies, Lambert, and Miller in the case of rank-2 lattices, where successive approximations of irrational numbers by rational numbers were shown to exhibit certain distribution patterns. This pattern indicates that among all rational numbers of height less than or equal to $n$, a significant proportion, namely one that asymptotically approaches $2^{n-1}$, can be expressed as sums of two square-rooted primes. Building upon this, the current research extends this outcome to a more complex scenario, where it demonstrates the $2^{n-1}$ proportion not only in the above-mentioned scenario but also in two additional situations, where certain pairs of numbers from a specific set are approximated to a precision of $n$, despite differing by a very small amount $\eta$. Notably, these new scenarios cover instances where $\eta$ is either extremely large or extremely small, where large is relative to $n$ and small is relative to a variable bound $C$, where a significant portion, asymptotically approaching $C^{n}$, of all relevant nut numbers exist within the specified conditions. A related outcome in the context of non-square lattice structures also shows that among all nut numbers of height less or equal to $n$,
We prove that for k-rational and k-Du Bois local complete interplays, they are k-equivalent.

Our experimental investigation focuses on a simple ferromagnetic substance made from the substance $^173$Yb and uses a technique to detect quantum properties in the substance by looking at the behavior of spin in the substance and how it reacts to an external magnetic field. By applying the Bragg principle on high-quality crystal samples, we found that the response to an external magnetic field results in the same phenomenon that causes the substance to transition from an ordered state to a disordered state at very low temperatures, known as the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thoules transition. Furthermore, we found that this external magnetic field also has an effect on the correlation length of the substance and results in an exponential increase in the substance's susceptibility at very low temperatures above the free ferromagnetic critical field.

If we consider the possibility that neutrinos have magnetic properties, it could lead to significant consequences, including the creation of hidden dark matter sectors and altered neutrino interactions. In particular, this phenomenon might give rise to a new class of ultralight, weakly-interacting particles, potentially explaining the galactic center's gamma-ray excess. Focusing on the axion-neutrino interaction, we investigate whether incorporating sterile neutrinos into the axion-like particle framework is beneficial. Within this extended framework, we determine the parameter space that accounts for the galactic center's gamma-ray excess, while also being consistent with local neutrino experiments and cosmic microwave background observations. Notably, the addition of sterile neutrinos enhances the predicted signals from the galactic center within this extended framework, potentially exceeding the observed excess levels. This modified approach also raises intriguing issues regarding dark matter segmentation and direct detection experiments. In general, this study underscores the significance of incorporating ultralight dark sectors into the standard model of particle physics, as they may involve light, feebly-interacting particles.

Research on the computational resources required by quantum circuits has led to significant breakthroughs, primarily due to the development of upper limits on the stabilizer rank of magic states. Specifically, the application of elliptic net methods has significantly improved our understanding, allowing for the extraction of quantum circuits that approximately achieve optimal resource consumption. Nevertheless, the current upper limits are still far from the predicted lower bounds, primarily because the existing upper limits exponentially grow with the circuit size. To address this, we have developed new upper limits on the stabilizer rank of magic states under certain constraints. Our research provides the first non-trivial upper limits for the stabilizer rank of symmetric magic states, and the associated generator matrices, which we show to be closed under a specific operation. Furthermore, we prove that a particular circuit can approximately implement the circuit Pauli-X approximation using stabilizer operations, and leverage this finding to enhance the stabilizer rank of magic states associated with circuits capable of approximating the Pauli-X operation.

We utilized the consideration of the Tsallis equation of state for the dark energy, which has led to the model's energy density displaying the property of power law decay. Consequently, we obtained the solution of the gravitational field equation in the presence of a cosmological constant, following which we calculated the expansion history, and found that the Tsallis holographic dark energy model adheres to the acceleration equation $\ddot{a}>0$, which indicates cosmic acceleration. Furthermore, we investigated phase transition, and plotted phase diagrams, which suggest that the model is feasible from a quantum instability standpoint when $\alpha>0$ and constrained by the thermal stability condition. Notably, the phase diagrams exhibit distinct behaviors based on the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$. Moreover, we investigated the cosmic naturalness of the model by calculating the decay width and finding the minimum value of the potential, which suggests that the model is cosmic natural, as the potential is bounded below.

The LAMOST time-domain survey began conducting systematic observations in March 2014 and is now publishing its initial results of observed targets from four $K$2 plates. These plates contain mostly main-sequence stars with or without exoplanets, but also other astrophysical objects such as active stars, late-type stars, and spectroscopic binaries. From the time-domain survey's first two observation cycles, we gathered four $K$2 plates and collected four epochs of data. To select variable and unique objects, we utilized the $p$-factor to screen candidate targets with distinct spectral features. Upon inspection, we validated the variability of 1888 objects and noted 1728 targets with notable spectral features across multiple observation periods. Furthermore, we extracted data on 2478 targets with consistent spectral features and analyzed their spectral characteristics. Our time-domain survey's initial outcomes demonstrate the value of ongoing monitoring of these variable and evolving stars, as well as extensive research on their spectral properties.

A novel technique has been proposed to create truly random numbers using SRAM cells by intentionally reducing the supply voltage below its nominal value.
This approach leverages the SRAM's inherent randomness caused by noise when it operates outside its designated voltage range, which in practice lies outside the range that the system's error correction mechanism can contain.
To mitigate this issue, a specialized circuitry is designed to limit operation within the stable memory region, while allowing data to be collected from a ring-orientated SRAM cell architecture that generates random bits.
The proposed system's performance and security have been evaluated under dynamic voltage and frequency scaling conditions.
The results show that even when subjected to varying supply voltages, the system's bitstream remains consistent in terms of bit error rate and entropy, thereby ensuring the generation of uniformly distributed random numbers.
Ultimately, the proposed technique can facilitate the creation of truly random numbers with exceptionally high quality, while also being resilient to system-level performance variations.

A new class of resistive switches has emerged, leveraging the adjustable properties of single molecules to regulate electrical current. To accelerate the development and advancement of this novel technology, detailed models describing how single molecules conduct electricity are needed. To this end, a series of molecules containing a central metal ion and flanking terthiophene layers have been investigated. By adjusting the energy levels between the highest occupied molecular orbital and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital, and also the position of the central metal ion's energy level, the conductance properties of these molecules can be finely tuned. As a result, the current voltage characteristics can be either non-rectifying or actively switched, depending on the desired application.

In particle physics, we use Feynman diagrams to represent interactions among particles. However, calculating certain subparts of these interactions, known as Feynman integrals, can become very complex. Despite the benefits of checkpointing, allowing us to pause and resume computations, many checkpoints become invalid when the integral is further simplified, rendering them useless. This problem persists in calculations involving multiple loops. To resolve this issue, we've developed a causal depiction of Feynman integrals, representing the underlying mathematical objects in a form that can be efficiently computed and modified. This goal is achieved by expressing Feynman integrals as sums of graphical elements, following a specific order in time. By reordering the particles' timing, the number of invalid checkpoints significantly decreases, and this approach extends to complex Feynman integrals with multiple loops. To confirm the effectiveness of this representation, we've evaluated the uncertainty of numerical results for 39 complex integrals, comparing the performance of different computation methods with or without the causal depiction.

A novel eigenvalue equation is formulated for one-dimensional two-level quantum walks with periodic coin functions, allowing for the calculation of eigenvalues via a discrete Fourier transform of the coin function. Furthermore, an eigenstate expansion formula is developed, revealing that the quantum walk's eigenstates can be expressed as a finite combination of stationary states associated with periodic wave functions. As a result, the support of such eigenstates only occurs at lattice points that are coprime to the coin function's period. We present specific examples of non-periodic coins and their associated eigenstates, demonstrating intricate patterns within the quantum walk's spectrum and eigenstate structures.

In this study, we investigate the properties of composite quark stars consisting of quarks, rhos, and antisymmetric matter, applying the sigma-omega-rho model, combined with the MIT and NJL models. We derive our results by solving the Einstein-Maxwell equations in conjunction with the quark-rho-antisymmetric matter equations. We then analyze the effects of Rho-mesons and cold dense matter on a compact star's global structure, specifically its mass-radius relation. Additionally, we examine the phase transition from neutron stars to quark stars and investigate the possibility of a third phase consisting of rho matter. Our findings indicate that the presence of Rho-mesons influences the thermal and thermal-magnetic equations, while a star's equation of state is largely determined by the interaction within the hadronic phase. It is discovered that Rho-mesons significantly alter a star's radius and the mass-radius relation, and could potentially explain the 2 solar mass observed by the TOROS project. Furthermore, we identified several sets of parameters in both models that allow for a phase transition from neutron stars to quark stars, and that support the possibility of a third phase consisting of rho matter. Our study also discovered that the phase transition from neutron stars to quark stars is heavily dependent on the characteristics of Rho-mesons and the coupling constant between Rho-mesons and other matter.

We explore the optical system of a $q$-deformed optomechanical configuration, where the movement of a mirror is influenced by its temperature and the presence of an input field in a multimode optical field. Utilizing the $|q\rangle$ deformed bosonic operator, the system is modeled and its Clarity function and entropy are examined. Our analysis reveals that for $q = 0$, the system behaves as a conventional optomechanical configuration. Notably, we observe that the entropy exhibits diurnal motion within the steady state and that the amplitude of this motion increases with an increase in anihilation number $N_0$. Furthermore, we examine the effect of $q$ on the clarity and find that even slight values can significantly degrade the optomechanical properties, suggesting their potential danger in such systems. Lastly, we propose that the value of $q$ could be experimentally determined by analyzing the system's transmission and reflecting properties.

In a model where an Slu and its dual R have a well-defined spin, it's suggested that R-parity-scissors modes could be severely suppressed. This is due to the fact that R-parity-scissors modes necessitate both the initial and final states having either both even or both odd R-parity properties, which is not supported by the Dual-Rotors model. As a result, R-parity-scissors transitions are expected to be significantly less frequent than superfluid transitions, leading to the hypothesis that R-parity-scissors modes might be absent or at least substantially subordinated to superfluid scissors modes. This could have major implications for our understanding of the low-lying wave functions in deformed nuclei.

during layer growth. This model reveals the stability criteria of different rotation
types and confirms that layer growth in these structures can be considered a classic
example of a layered phase, with each layer acting as a quantum. The model's findings
also explain the phenomenon of orbital variations within these films.

We're examining static and dynamic phenomena in a laser-cooled atomic system arranged in an optical lattice structure dissipated by internal photon scattering. This interatomic photon-scattering process produces a gentle repulsive force among the atoms,, thus deviating from conventional Boltzmann-Gazza statistics. Consequently, unusual particle number distributions, correlations, and entropies result. Specifically, for the Boltzmann-Gazza statistics, we've developed a growth curve for particle correlations in the equilibrium state. Additionally, we've observed oscillations in particle correlations following a sudden removal of the repulsive force, along with an exponential decay of these oscillations. Our research confirms that these oscillations can persist for an infinite duration in the limit where the atoms' initial energies are minimal.

This study investigates the extent to which higher-order relationships among cryptocurrency trading pairs exist, beyond the conventional pair-wise connections. Our findings indicate that the cryptocurrency market is characterized by complex interaction patterns. To achieve this, we employed a Bayesian network to analyze the relationships among cryptocurrency trading pairs. By utilizing a discrete symmetrical network structure, we observed significant non-zero dependencies among pairs. Subsequently, a validation test was performed on our results using a random model. Our findings also reveal that higher-order relationships among cryptocurrency trading pairs do exist and that these patterns are enduring. To quantify the intensity of these relationships, we developed a novel metric measuring the strength of interactions and leveraged this to distinguish between cryptocurrency trading pairs with significant higher-order connections and those with only pair-wise links.

By employing high-level path-integrated Monte Carlo post-simulation analysis, the properties of small (H$_2$O)$_m$(H$_2$S)$_n$ clusters with $m+n=1-5$ and $m \geq 1$ were examined at temperature $T=295$ K, utilizing a potential energy surface that includes vibrational contributions. The results showed that including the effects of zero-point motion significantly altered the interatomic radial distribution functions, largely by reducing the height and width of peak O...S at $r \approx 2.6$ A, and led to the formation of smaller (H$_2$O)$_m$(H$_2$S) clusters with stronger hydrogen bonds between acid and water molecules. Furthermore, while acid molecules preferentially bonded to the surface of water clusters, those formed at higher concentrations or through exchange showed a notable increase in isolated H$_2$S dimer formations. The outcomes suggest that the impact of vibrational effects should not be disregarded in modeling the chemistry of acid-water clusters.

We suggest compiling an ordered list of binary recognition pairs $(A, B)$ based on their equivalence under group actions, with the goal of leveraging compactification techniques to gain insights into the resulting spaces of functions that map $(A \times B)$ to non-negative values. Our study focuses particularly on spaces of functions that exhibit group compatibility and a specific fixed cost property in relation to the recognition distance. These function spaces find practical applications in tasks such as recognizing group-action invariant objects.

The relationship between heat and momentum in quantized systems exhibits distinct behaviors at absolute zero and finite temperatures. For systems with chiral excitations, this relationship reduces to a simple proportion at zero temperature, which breaks down into an intricate correlation at higher temperatures. We observed a comparable response in the thermal momentum of certain superconducting/pseudo-symmetric materials and granular metals, which indeed shows a comparable Einstein's proportion at lower temperatures. However, in both cases, this breakdown into a more intricate correlation occurs at higher temperatures relative to the respective characteristic energy scales of these materials.

In various machine learning tasks, the inherent organization of data often results in models being trained that capture essential patterns. Our investigation seeks to explain how neural networks typically prefer simpler representations over more complex ones. While the importance of regularization in model selection is well-documented, our analysis reveals that the regularizing effect in geometric complexity comes primarily from multiple constraints imposed by data organization. Focusing on well-structured data sets, we demonstrate that neural networks naturally incorporate principles of data organization that lead to fewer decision boundaries, resulting in lower generalization errors. This is evident across different data distributions, including uniform, Gaussian, and isotonic scenarios. Furthermore, we observe that geometric complexity regularizers significantly improve performance even in cases of randomly initialized networks. Our findings also suggest that such complexity regularizers are unique to organized data sets and can be quantified using metrics such as Calibani's calibance.

New constraints are derived for six Wilson coefficients within the Standard Model using data on fully reconstructed $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays, selected from a larger sample provided by LHCb. The analysis utilizes flavor conservation in $B^0\to K^{*0}$ decays to mitigate biases and uncertainties, allowing for more precise calculations. The new results align with existing experimental findings and are consistent with theoretical predictions from model-independent analysis and perturbative QCD.

The widespread adoption of Transformer-based models in NLP tasks has been facilitated in part by data augmentation techniques that have enabled them to match and even surpass the performance of traditional architectures previously considered to be more robust. This paper examines the data augmentation methods used with Transformer-based models in the context of Automated Essay Grading (AEG) to understand why they achieve better results than architectures previously considered superior in this specific task. By investigating the data augmentation techniques used for training Transformer-based models in AEG, we will identify the most effective methods and explain their benefits. Additionally, we will explain how these techniques can potentially lead to adverse effects, including the production of low-quality training data that may guide the model away from accurate outcomes in this particular task.

The area of marginal dependence models is primarily concerned with the analysis of univariate time series. Despite this, the literature often incorporates models that rely on an implicit common underlying process, thereby restricting their practical applications. This study aims to provide a comprehensive framework for marginal dependence models, critiquing existing methods and offering a new metric to assess temporal relationships within a single series, which adapts to various cases where multiple factors are involved. The proposed framework then transitions to common factor models, focusing on the estimation of common parameters, while allowing the unobserved factors to remain latent. The main contribution here is the development of a test statistics to assess the relevance of individual series to common factors, thereby facilitating series selection. The methodology is then demonstrated through applications to both artificial and real data.

A theoretical model of social mobility is presented, where multiple groups of young individuals compete for a limited number of positions that carry out opportunities, and the eligible population expands and contracts over time. Under specific conditions, a variable represents how these opportunities are distributed among different groups and the model becomes a continuous-time process. As positions become available, they are allocated to the group with the highest rate of successful advancement or, in cases of tie-ups, the group that experienced the longest wait time, resulting in a significant increase in the group's size. However, since the model does not have an obvious general solution, two approximate methods are proposed to analyze the distribution of opportunities. The first method relies on the model's behavior near complete systems, while the second uses a large-systems limit, reducing the distribution of opportunities to a probability distribution that depends on the groups' mean sizes. Both methods result in the same distribution, which in turn, depends on the groups' mean sizes and the model's parameters, and this distribution has the property of being continuous and decreasing in the fraction of available positions. With the number of positions relatively small compared to the total number of young individuals, the distribution of opportunities is highly concentrated in a relatively small number of groups, primarily confined to a small set of these groups, especially when the mean sizes of the groups are relatively similar. This result is independent of the model's parameters, the definition of group sizes, and even the groups' classification. This finding is particularly true when there are

The symmetry of wavefunctions under parity for particles of arbitrary spin is responsible for determining the particle's statistics. For non-relativistic particles, the symmetry of wavefunctions under parity is the primary basis for determining the particle's statistics, as described by a spherical tensor operator. This results in bosonic statistics for particles with integer spin and fermionic statistics for particles with half-integer spin. This approach can be taken as the foundation for deriving the spin-statistics connection.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented, which we subsequently test through benchmarking analysis.
While Delegated RingCT may not possess the same level of anonymity compared to other RingCT implementations or even centralised cryptocurrencies such as Monero, it can provide a suitable balance of anonymity and transaction efficiency for use in sidechains or private versions of toll roads, or as a middle ground in scenarios where full decentralisation is not required.

The space complexity of solving general linear equations can be reduced to nearly logarithmic complexity by utilizing nearly linear equation solvers, which require only n*log(k) operations, where k is the number of non-zero rows in the matrix. Building on Chor and Smolensky's (1988) idea of randomized solving, we present a new algorithm that exploits the properties of small-space solvers to achieve a significant decrease in space usage, from O(n) to O(log(n)), with only a limited increase in time, from O(n*log(log(k))) to O(n*log(k)*log(n)). By applying this solution to random linear equations, we demonstrate that solving such equations becomes feasible in small-space settings, where they were previously shown to be impossible to solve, even in large-space settings, provided the coefficient distribution meets certain criteria. Notably, our solution is compatible with existing linear equation solvers, including those based on the Planted Submatrix Problem, which enables us to achieve a breakthrough in space usage, from O(n^(1/4)) to O(log(n)), while only increasing the time by a polynomial factor, where previously the best known solution had a time complexity of O(n^(5/4)).

In certain theoretical models exceeding the standard model, large-scale particle collisions have potential links to early universe events, such as the creation of heavy particles and symmetry-breaking processes. This study investigates the possibility of producing heavy gauge bosons in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV and identifies detectable production mechanisms yielding three gauge bosons. Numerical simulations within the standard model and its extensions, specifically a left-right model, are conducted to determine observable signals at the Large Hadron Collider. Results indicate that while triboelectric effects are detectable with anticipated detection limits of around 0.8-1.1 pb, they do not exceed LHC capabilities. Conversely, left-right model predictions exhibit significantly higher production rates, largely attributed to non-standard model interactions, roughly two orders of magnitude higher than triboelectric effects, reaching levels of around 15-17 fb, heavily surpassing LHC detection limits.

In 2019, Hebrew joined the Universal Dependencies project, with a treebank developed from the Israeli constituent lattice bank, primarily consisting of written texts. This paper reports on the update to UD 2.7, incorporating new annotations and removing early errors. Additionally, the study revisits Hebrew parsing performance, finding it inferior to other languages and identifying domain-specific challenges. To improve parsing, a new task and dataset, COMPAS-HE, have been created, with tasks and data developed in collaboration with Israel's National Library. COMPAS-HE combines instruction and knowledge formation with the help of expert librarians.

We establish that for any fixed $1 < p < \infty$ and $M > 0$, there exists an $M$-independent dimension $n(M)$ and a probability measure $\mu$ on the standard $\ell_p$ space such that $\mu$ does not compress to a finite-dimensional subspace of $\ell_p$ and the $\varepsilon$-isometry distance between $\mu$ and its image under a given $\varepsilon$-isometry on $\ell_p$ exceeds $n(M)/2$. This distance is defined as the minimum number of $\varepsilon$-isometry operations required to achieve the transformation. Our work builds upon a previous result by Krasnyuk, who showed that the distance between two distinct invariant measures on the Heisenberg group has a linear lower bound under an $\varepsilon$-isometry. In our case, the lower bound on the transformation distance exhibits a linear increase with $\varepsilon$. Our method of proof involves constructing a directed graph of finite-dimensional $\ell_p$ spaces and showing that for a specified Dirac measure and an associated iterative algorithm, which adds newly $\varepsilon$-isometric images to a growing set of spaces, there exists a point of discontinuity in the graph where the algorithm's behavior changes under an increasing sequence of $\varepsilon$. This point determines our probability measure $\mu$ such that it cannot be compressed to a finite-dimensional subspace of

Recent advancements in physics-informed neural networks have led to novel numerical methods that seamlessly integrate analytical models with adaptive neural network models. However, these methods predominantly rely on established physical laws and are primarily designed to solve initial-value problems. This research extends the concept of physics-informed neural networks to tackle complex problems involving mixed initial/boundary value problems, especially fluid-plate interactions, while incorporating collaborative filtering techniques from statistics to mitigate the dimensionality curse and produce sample-specific results. The proposed algorithm, collaborative physics-informed neural networks, utilizes neural networks to approximate the solution and its derivative, side-stepping expensive numerical differentiators. The approach yields high-quality solutions at a low computational cost, outperforming conventional methods in terms of both precision and speed.

This study proposes an innovative construction method for designing robust, error-correcting low-density parity-check codes intended for operation in a binary erasure channel with potential applications in flash memory technology. Our code design is influenced by the 'degree-degree diagram' parameter, which serves as an analytical tool for assessing code performance. By systematically examining the properties of degree sequences in bipartite graphs representing the codes, we establish a clear framework for designing the codes. Our results indicate that codes with evenly distributed degrees and those based on irregular repeat accumulate codes perform particularly well under the degree-degree diagram criterion, thereby providing a practical design approach for creating robust low-density parity-check codes capable of withstanding severe channel conditions and accommodating large numbers of channels.

A novel digital security filter, designed for adaptive signal processing systems, uses system-level synthesis to create a secure analogue output from an insecure digital input. This secure filter, based on an ALMA-based algorithm, can effectively counteract control mechanisms' vulnerabilities to manipulation. By employing a cryptographic code and an irregular electrical connection, the circuit's resistive feedback resistors are randomly set, generating unpredictable analogue dynamics in the output signal. The analytical framework developed, yielding tight bounds on the Hermite interpolating series, enables the data rate and processing delay of the secure filter to be quantitatively assessed. Experimental results confirm that the new security filter prevents control mechanisms from being manipulated while maintaining functional connectivity to the input signal.

A critical component in quantum key exchange protocols is the ability to confirm that a long-distance channel is secure. However, this issue remains unresolved in previous studies, which discovered that an untrusted attacker could potentially exploit flaws in random phase encoding to hijack the exchange. To address this concern, a modified version of the key exchange protocol has been developed, employing a hybrid approach that combines random phase encoding with specific measurement states and decoy states to enhance security. Through analysis, it was determined that this enhanced protocol can withstand hacking attacks, including those involving sophisticated predictions of photon states, and remain resilient against quantitative entanglement attacks. What's more, it appears that an untrusted attacker's advantages in hacking are significantly diminished by the protocol's safeguards, thereby safeguarding the entire exchange process and confirming that the long-distance channel is secure.

Recent studies have suggested several factors might influence a large language model's performance when performing "in-context" learning, including the diversity of its pretraining data and the presence of categories within that data. In this research, we explored whether these factors truly impact a large language model's performance, or if its superior performance is solely attributed to its ability to generalize based on the first few examples provided. A large-scale linguistic model was used to investigate four learning paradigms, utilizing datasets of varying size and domain diversity. The results contradicted previous expectations, showing the model performed best on datasets most closely related to its pretraining data, despite initial evidence suggesting the model could adapt to novel domains. The model's strong performance in those closely related domains may be the result of overfitting to its pretraining data, rather than any inherent ability to generalize.

Galaxy cluster observations have highlighted the importance of cooling flows, which can lead to unique galaxy growth. To investigate the fragmentation and growth of galaxies in cooling flows, we conducted three-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations that took into account cosmic magnetic fields, the cosmic microwave background, and electron thermal conduction. The results showed that the number of galaxies formed in a cooling flow depends on the strength of magnetic fields and initial cloud density. Strong magnetic fields delay the growth of galaxies by inhibiting the growth of massive galaxies and promoting the growth of small ones. High cloud density inhibits the growth of galaxies by limiting accretion and enhances star formation, resulting in fewer galaxies with higher star formation rates. The effect of thermal conduction and the cosmic microwave background on galaxy formation is negligible, primarily because it occurs far from these processes. The effect of magnetic fields persists throughout the formation of galaxies, determined by the strength of magnetic fields and properties of clouds, which can result in the growth of galaxies across a broad mass range.

The observed anomalies in the charm sector, specifically excesses seen in $D^0$ and $D^{\pm}$ decays and lack of same-sign lepton events in $B_{(s)}$ meson decays, are investigated. We note that, although these anomalies reside in different sectors governed by CKM theory, they exhibit a notable discrepancy of one order of magnitude. Furthermore, we explore the possibility that these anomalies could be related, potentially facilitated by an imaginary component in the charm unitary triangle, induced by new physics. We establish that the observed anomalies can be reconciled if the CP violations in $D^0$ and $D^{\pm}$ decays and $B^0_s$ decay exhibit discrepancies of one order of magnitude greater than current values. In the case of $B^0$ decay, the discrepancy is not constrained by this analysis. We emphasize that these predictions do not necessarily imply the magnitude of these anomalies is solely new physics-driven, as they may also be influenced by existing physics factors.

New high-loops scalar particle collision amplitudes have been calculated in superstring theory. These amplitudes, which are compatible with the Gross conjecture, reveal a relationship between bosonic and fermionic particle collision amplitudes. Furthermore, the calculated bosonic amplitudes demonstrate a connection to the Cayley tree graph, illustrating the presence of non-trivial interactions among particles.

To efficiently manage the growing traffic across densely deployed devices such as IoT sensors and smart gadgets, future networks require strategic resource management. To achieve this, network functions need to be dynamically adjusted based on real-time data availability, necessitating real-time resource monitoring and instant decision-making. To address these challenges, this paper proposes the integration of Virtualized Network Functions (VNFs) based on Software Defined Networking (SDN) principles and Cloud Computing. To optimize traffic flow and meet increasing demand, an optimization algorithm is also implemented, which takes into account the placement of VNFs and device scheduling to minimize end-user delay. Notably, the paper focuses on the sustainability and self-organizing capabilities of 5G networks in terms of resource management and energy efficiency, presenting an innovative model using IoT sensors and micro-data centers, which are then optimized using a cloud-based SDN approach.

The goal of zero-speech voice synthesis is to create a voice model that can be trained without access to speech data, instead using a text corpus and a small set of transcriptions derived from actual speech. These transcriptions are generated by mapping character-based text to auditory units such as tone of voice, pitch, and duration, which are then sequenced in a way that is consistent with natural speech. When trained on these transcriptions, the voice model can produce high-quality speech that matches the input of the transcriptions. In our study, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach and compare it to other methods of voice synthesis, revealing that the quality of the synthesized speech is comparable to that of speech that has been directly translated from text to speech. Additionally, we have made our transcription tool publicly available, as well as a corresponding voice model, both of which can be used to perform zero-speech voice synthesis.

Optimizing motion planning within complex environments necessitates efficient optimization techniques that can balance performance with computational feasibility. Convex optimization offers a valuable tool, but its application is limited by the linearization accuracy of the underlying system models. To overcome this hurdle, a novel approach deploys data-driven McCormick evaluation complexes to facilitate multi-stage combined convex programming. By leveraging the characteristics of motion planning, a specialized formulation is designed to incorporate these complexes, thereby enhancing the potential solution space. Furthermore, the algorithm's multi-stage design empowers decision-makers to prioritize current objectives over long-term considerations. The proposed framework is then evaluated through its application to a satellite orbit maintenance problem. The results demonstrate that this approach yields a substantial enhancement in solution quality, with a notable improvement of at least one order of magnitude in optimal cost, and at least two orders of magnitude in terms of feasible trajectory numbers, compared to a standard MPC scheme.

In the class of probabilistic convertibility of quantum states, there are specific resource limitations inherent in near-deterministic transformability. A crucial factor is the predictability of the process, which largely depends on the resource quality. By utilizing the concept of resource distillation, we prove that the near-deterministic transformability of a particular state, when achieved through a specific set of operations (LOCC), can be restricted by the following condition: it does not have a certain resource, now termed rPD-rapidly-distillable-resource, if it can be efficiently transformed into another state with high accuracy (strictly better than random) using LOCC. By virtue of this condition, we demonstrate that a particular set of resources, comprising near-deterministically transformable states, and its distillable forms, forms an ordered sequence. Furthermore, our findings also imply that a particular form of quantum operation, termed PD-operations, is not only limited in its ability to achieve maximum predictability of near-deterministic transforms, but also, in general, cannot be equivalent to deterministic transforms, even when augmented by certain additional operations.

We investigated the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being carried while in motion, by treating its contents as a nonlinear oscillator. The liquid in the cup forms a cylindrical shape when it moves, which allows us to determine the angular frequency and energy of the oscillation. By considering the precession of the cone as a shift in the oscillation's phase, we established a relationship between the angular frequency of the oscillation and the fluid's surface tension, as well as the gravity and curvature of the container. The formed cone's shape also influenced the oscillation's movement, which resulted in two types of movements: a primary vibration and a secondary vibration that occurred when the cone's apex deviated from its normal position. An experimental test confirmed our findings, and the model presented here provides a framework for describing the complex movement of liquid in a rotating cup.

In the decentralized learning setting, a central server facilitates client training and communicates with them via message exchange. However, existing research has revealed that decentralized learning is susceptible to data privacy breaches and biased learning outcomes due to the reliance on sensitive client data and imperfect communication channels. To address these challenges, we introduce a new robust decentralized learning algorithm called DR-DSGD, which leverages the concept of distributionally robust learning to minimize bias and does not require sharing client data. By applying a non-expectation approach to our proposed DR-DSGD, we demonstrate that it converges at a rate of O(1/t) and is applicable in various real-world scenarios, including graph-based networks.

Relativistic nuclear collisions produce particle flows that can be described using a low-frequency approximation of relativistic hydrodynamics.  In this approximation, effective pullers are described by the speed of sound $c_s$, which is less than the speed of light.  We investigate how individual $c_s$ values contribute to the final stage of relativistic hydrodynamics and examine the constraints on $c_s$ throughout the spacetime.  We also explore how individual $c_s$ values affect the production of charged particles.  Additionally, we are investigating how varying the initial state energy density influences $c_s$ and charged particle production.  We found that even with small changes in energy density, $c_s$ remains largely unaffected, but these modifications can lead to variations in produced charged particles.  We observed that increasing the number of $c_s$ values does not significantly alter the overall production of charged particles but can shift their yields towards lower or higher values.  We are comparing our findings to existing experimental data and exploring how our results can be applied to the QCD theory.

We conduct a detailed analysis of the connection between a powerful protostellar jet and slower moving outflows from a massive star-forming system, Class 0 object IRAS 04191+0809. High-speed jets emanating from the core, comprising of fast-moving knots and jet plasma, are undetectable when they reach distances of more than 0.06 parsecs from the source, but become apparent at shorter distances of about 0.02 parsecs. It's observed that the low-velocity outflows, which were initially assumed to originate from the jet's interaction with surrounding material, could actually be produced by the resolution of high-speed knots into slower moving outflows. If this theory holds true, then it's possible that high-speed jets from core can drive low-velocity outflows over considerable distances without needing to interact with surrounding material, and also account for the decline in jet speed over time, and the variation in speed within the high-speed jet itself.

To maintain optimal performance and ensure safe operation, equilibrium between these two considerations is necessary. However, achieving this balance is challenging, especially in systems with performance limitations. This study provides a framework for simultaneously addressing these two goals, which involves formulating them as separate optimization problems subject to specific constraints. The proposed method, which leverages the system's steady-state behavior, enables effective regulation of nonlinear systems with performance constraints. The proposed strategy outperforms alternative control techniques, which prioritize either performance or safety, and is better suited for systems with uncertain parameters and limited observability. The approach is validated through applications to two complex systems: a simulation model of a thermocoustic driver and a pilot-controlled helicopter equipped with autonomous ground-coupled technology.

This research project seeks to delve into the family of semi-secular resonances resulting from the interaction between an object in orbit around the Sun and its gravitational influence. Initially, a mathematical framework will be established to identify and analyze these resonances. Subsequently, two numerical methods will be developed to provide precise approximations for the resonant frequencies and associated periodic orbits. Specifically, one approach will utilize analytical tools to find orbit solutions, whereas another method will leverage Birkhoff normal form techniques to determine these same objects in space.

A new approach is developed to study the symmetry properties of finite tight-binding models used to simulate light-matter interactions. This methodology, which leverages the existing framework of second-quantization, enhances the model's symmetry by incorporating a comprehensive Augmenting Algebraic Model. This model's symmetry properties are analogous to their continuum counterparts, allowing for a precise comparison. It is demonstrated that the model's symmetry properties remain intact even in the presence of non-zero velocities and diamagnetic terms. However, a subtle issue arises from the velocity operator's quadratic nature, which breaks certain symmetry expectations. Despite this limitation, the model's symmetry properties can still be utilized to develop simplified diagonal dispersion-based models that effectively describe a wide range of semiconductor materials, including their transition from direct to indirect bandgap behavior.

In computer vision, recognizing objects within a specific category is crucial across various applications, however existing solutions often fail to achieve low error rates, especially when dealing with objects from specific categories such as lamps or chairs. Existing benchmarks including the COCO challenge, focus solely on object detection and not enough on objects' spatial relationships or forms, limiting the development of category-level perception. To address this issue, we create a resilient benchmark using a large train set derived from Product Dataset and an ideal benchmark from real-world datasets. Our benchmark tests the accuracy of object pose and form estimation under various scenarios, both with and without potential errors in data collection and labeling. Our study reveals that current models fall short in providing accurate results for objects within specific categories and that even with perfect data, models may not reach their full potential without model redesign. Our work serves as a baseline for researchers to improve category-level perception and develop more robust models adapting to real-world challenges.

This study develops methods to estimate the parameters of Cauchy distributions, both individually and simultaneously, providing associated confidence intervals that account for bias. A sample of n data points is used to create these estimates and the associated intervals, utilizing the sample's median as a pivotal quantity. The methods proposed share similarities with those already established for normal distributions, offering ease of implementation that does not rely on specific software or programming. The study's findings are supported through simulations, examining the bias and variability of the estimators and confidence intervals, particularly how they perform for small data sets.

In the context of basket trials, our method allows for the assessment of disease subtype magnitudes through a Bayesian approach, enabling simultaneous magnitude and error estimation. By modeling subtypes as binary outcomes and assuming they draw from separate, unknown distributions, our method determines how likely each subtype is to occur and how they divide. When one subtype is entirely absent, our approach includes a data borrowing component, facilitating borrowing between subtypes and ensuring continuity. As the number of disease subtypes increases, our method resembles traditional Bayesian binary sample size calculation. The desired type I error rate and the desired power are set as input parameters to illustrate our method's functionality. A basket trial is artificially constructed and analyzed using our method to demonstrate its application in clinical trials.

High-accuracy motion systems are susceptible to external disturbances which, if not adequately addressed, can significantly limit their operational capabilities. The techniques employed to counter these effects often prioritize simplicity over accuracy in their design. Nevertheless, when external disturbances are considered as parameter variations, more sophisticated approaches such as parameter-dependent controller designs can greatly improve performance. The key challenge in implementing such designs lies in the identification of sensitive system parameters. To overcome this issue, this paper proposes a novel method using a sequential loop closing algorithm that estimates relevant parameters and evaluates their impact on system performance, ultimately facilitating the development of improved motion systems. The proposed method is tested and validated using a simulation of a precise motion system.

We introduce a general, flexible framework called Partial Registration Network (PRNet), designed to handle complex object alignment challenges. PRNet takes in partial point cloud views of two objects and outputs corresponding latent features, which are then paired to generate corresponding features. A registration module in PRNet leverages these paired features to determine the relative transformation between the two views. PRNet employs Self-Guided Learning (SGL) to refine latent features through feedback mechanisms and a contrastive loss. This approach enables partial-to-partial registration for the first time, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods on object alignment tasks. We expand on existing methods by adding new metrics, updating the evaluation protocol to include more accurate measures, and introduce code to support these changes. We also conduct additional experiments to validate our results.

A group G is deemed R_infinity characteristic if the R_infinity property, initially defined by Dru\accent23, exhibits uniqueness and exclusivity. In simpler terms, this means no non-trivial subgroup of G possesses the R_infinity property. In this study, we establish that numerous nilpotent quotients of generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups (specifically those denoted as GS(n,1), with n being any non-zero integer value) are R_infinity characteristic. Furthermore, we also identify the nitely presented nilpotent quotients of these groups as R_infinity characteristic as well. Additionally, a key aspect of our work involves presenting an algorithmic tool, the NilQuoter, which enables the generation of nilpotent quotients for (n,1) groups based on finite presentations. By using the NilQuoter, we manually constructed the R_infinity characteristic quotients for specific (n,1) groups and also employed it to detect the R_infinity characteristic nature in countless non-Abelian nilpotent (n,1) groups, particularly those with nilpotency class 3. Consequently, our findings indicate that the R_infinity characteristic trait is inherently linked to certain non-Abelian nilpotent (n,1) groups possessing class 3. In fact, we propose the conjecture that this relationship might be extensive, encompassing all non-Abelian nilpotent (n,1) groups with class

The sensitivity of various hypothetical particle colliders to indicators of SM instability is evaluated using quantitative measures. Compared to other options, future hadron colliders are found to offer the most robust evidence of SM instability. In particular, even a 33 teV hadron collider with 5 ab^-1 integrated luminosity and 10 ab^-1 electron/positron combined luminosity at 250 geV would still be capable of detecting SM instability, assuming no abnormal production mechanisms exist.

To estimate the resonance allocation amplitudes of $D^*$ and $D^*_s$, the resonances $D^*(2007)$ and $D^*_s(2112)$, our analysis uses Bethe-Salpeter wave functions. The calculation employs nonrelativistic quark models, specifically the potential model and the instanton model, to determine the amplitudes. The potential model, accounting for quark movement, yields amplitudes 0.71, 0.47 for $D^*(2007)$, while the instanton model gives amplitudes 0.69, 0.35 for $D^*_s(2112)$.

The research defines the Gelfand-Shilov space $\mathcal{S}^(\gamma)_\sigma$ and its variant $\mathcal{S}^(\gamma)_\sigma\langle\langle M\rangle\rangle$ within the context of tempered distributions. Key findings include alternative formulations of these spaces in terms of Fourier analysis and the nontriviality of certain ideal Banach algebras associated with them. Additionally, the investigation establishes relationships between the original Gelfand-Shilov spaces and these variants, also providing counterexamples to demonstrate the un uniqueness of certain Toeplitz operators.

Recent findings suggest that training a model using data from only a single view is sufficient to obtain satisfactory results, eliminating the need for labeled samples. However, as our work demonstrates, view diversity is crucial and view-specific fine-tuning may be necessary to achieve optimal results. Notably, existing methods struggle when dealing with unlabeled data across multiple views, resulting in subpar performance. To address this limitation, we propose the CPGAN technique, leveraging an adversarial training model that utilizes a partitioning mechanism to segment unlabeled data into distinct views. By focusing on each view's internal structure, CPGAN is able to generate instances that accurately match their respective distributions, resulting in superior performance across a range of datasets, outperforming competing methods by a significant margin.

Research in natural language processing has focused on determining word order
in sentences and then employing recurrent neural networks to generate human-readable
output. Conversely, this paper's goal is to forecast a user's action in a
communication system. We propose an innovative, feature-extraction RNN architecture
capable of transforming variable-length action histories into fixed-length feature
vectors. In doing so, an action selection module can easily utilize these features
via a simple comparison with existing classes. To facilitate efficient feature
extraction, this paper presents an innovative RNN-based model, incorporating a
radial basis function (RBF) kernel. Evaluations of our proposed model on a
communication dataset demonstrate superior performance over multiple benchmark
baselines.

The analysis of a rare and dramatic celestial occurrence known as a great flare is presented. The analysis presents a detailed computational model of the near ultraviolet spectral ranges observed during the great flare of AD Leo in 1985, and the results are compared to observations of another flare of similar characteristics in SDSS J163738.03+252624 and to observations of solar flares. The computer model used to create the spectral ranges is based on the magnetic interaction between two rotating stars of equal mass, and the rotation speeds of the stars are set to the range of 1 to 100 kilometers per second. The computer model includes ten spectral lines, and the width of these lines is set to one kilometer per second. The computer simulation successfully reproduced the spectral ranges of the great flare of AD Leo in 1985, and the results are that the rotation speeds of the stars in the system are between 20 and 200 kilometers per second. The computer model used to create the spectral ranges is applicable to a wide range of celestial occurrences known as T Tauri stars and is capable of explaining two patterns of rotation that are observed in these occurrences. The computer model is also applicable to the analysis of the great flare of SDSS J163738.03+252624, and the results are that the rotation speeds of the stars in this system are between 20 and 200 kilometers per second. We carry out a study of deformations of G2 instantons on nearly G2 manifolds. By translating the nearly G2 structure along a vector field and exploiting the deformation equation's linearization, we find that the deformation space of a G2 instanton is isomorphic to the first cohomology group of the complex of real vector forms with a twisted differential. Furthermore, we establish that the first real Chern form of a G2 instantons' deformation complex corresponds to the Nijenhuis tensor associated with the almost product structure derived from the nearly G2 structure. Additionally, we examine how the deformation of a G2 instanton influences the associated characteristic form and describe the relationship between the real and complex forms' cohomologies.

The category of one-to-one harmonic mappings between complex spaces has been further divided into subcategories denoted by $C(\lambda,\mu)$, where the use of contracted image domains is taken into consideration. This research investigates whether a harmonic mapping, initially defined on a half-plane and exhibiting $C$-normality when applied to functions within $H^2$, can be mapped bi-holomorphically to its contracted image. Our findings indicate that if a function, initially defined on a half-plane and exhibiting $C$-normality when applied to functions within $H^2$, can be mapped bi-holomorphically to its contracted image, then it must be univalent. Conversely, if a function that is sufficiently smooth exhibits $C$-normality when applied to functions within $H^2$ and remains bi-holomorphic upon contraction, then it possesses a specific growth constraint. This research further finds that if a function, initially defined on a half-plane and exhibiting $C$-normality when applied to functions within $H^2$, can be mapped bi-holomorphically to its contracted image, then its conjugate must also be bi-holomorphic upon contraction, provided certain additional conditions are met.
