The composition of a planet is closely tied to its formation processes, making it a crucial feature to determine when studying planetary development. Previous studies have focused on gas giant planets, but there's a need to determine the composition of smaller, terrestrial-type planets to better understand their building blocks. We've developed a novel method using published data to determine the core-to-mass ratios, metal contents, and silicate compositions of stars that host these planets. This way, we can infer the planetary bodies' mass ranges, metallicity levels, and surface compositions. Applying our method to a sample of 107 stars that host terrestrial planets, we found a range of core-to-mass ratios in stars that host planets in the habitable zone or small planets, with higher metal contents than those with large planets in eccentric orbits. Notably, we found that stars with planets having higher metal contents than those without. Furthermore, we determined that planets with masses of around 2 Earth masses have diameters similar to those of the Rocky planets, and typically have crusts and mantles similar to those of the Earth, but with differences in metal contents. However, we found no correlation between planetary mass, orbit, or stellar metallicity in determining planetary core sizes. These findings indicate that core formation theories and planetary building processes are highly diverse.

Currently, Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) that use Channel State Information (CSI) for locating devices in Wireless Localized Systems (WLS) consider all CSI data equally, thus overlooking redundant or irrelevant data. We propose Attention-based CSI WLS, which selects key CSI to use for better performance. It applies a deep network to extract features from the selected CSI, then calculates the signal strength of the determined location. The model is optimized using contrastive learning and is trained end-to-end. Experimental results show that Attention-based CSI WLS outperforms other methods by 9.5% in terms of accuracy. Additionally, it requires less CSI, resulting in a 30% reduction in calculation complexity.

This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of various modal logics by incorporating their associated modal operators within enhanced topological structures. Different types of modalities are dissected and their underlying topological properties are defined. According to the type, modalities either pertain to a single point (point-like), allowing reference to a location itself, or they extend over a locale (spread-like), enabling mention of the surrounding topological structure. Several topological structures are examined, including pretopological, semipretopological, and uniform spaces, each accompanied by a distinct collection of point-like and locale-based modalities. The topological theorems in these contexts are shown to be equivalent to theorems in the respective modal logics, while additionally possessing an intuitive categorical interpretation that reflects their soundness and completeness.

In 2007, Khuller and Mulder introduced the concept of edge-tinted paths within bipartite graphs, aiming to replicate the properties of the traveling salesman problem on these graphs. This involved determining whether a bipartite graph with distinct edge weights containing a Birkhoff polytope vertex, specifically a point on the k-cubical polytope, could be approximated by an edge-tinted path with a weighted path less than k times longer. Mulder later posed the question of establishing, at the very least, a linear approximation. Our study counteracts even the simplest form of linear approximation, as we demonstrate a scenario where the approximation ratio is at least linear.

We investigate the minimum thresholds of functions on the Hamming graphs of arbitrary dimensions that exhibit specific symmetry properties and are either even or odd in nature. Our work is particularly focused on determining these minimum thresholds under two distinct parameter settings: (i) when the Fourier coefficients of the functions are confined to a limited number of frequencies, and (ii) when the functions are evaluated up to a particular frequency. Our findings involve establishing inequalities relating the maximum possible values of eigenvalues and the norms of functions, which in turn enable us to derive precise minimum thresholds in both scenarios.

COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, but previous efforts to enhance user interaction were hindered by limitations in coding and user libraries. To address this, a new web-based interface, ShinyCOPASI, has been developed using the R language to provide a more interactive and responsive experience. This platform offers a suite of widgets and tools to explore and visualize model results, track simulations, and identify key dynamic characteristics. Additionally, it features a module selection system, enabling users to customize their workflow and save models, operations, and parameters for later use.

In recent years, various approaches to quantifying ambiguity in machine learning models have emerged, but a comprehensive evaluation of these methods has not been conducted. This study groups ambiguity quantification techniques into four categories and reviews existing metrics within each group, providing a framework for analyzing models' ambiguity levels. By systematically assessing the metrics' statistical properties, this study examines their reliability in the context of 35 methods across seven categories. These categories include output-based, input-based, semi-supervised, deep learning-based, ensemble, graph-based, and cluster-based ambiguity measures. A thorough investigation of the metrics' strengths and weaknesses, as well as suggestions for future research, is also provided.

We're investigating the von Neumann algebra resulting from the set of type functions on a compact quantum group. The type of a unitary representation is defined as the difference between its highest and lowest dimension. The central subset of type functions corresponds to integral weights and, consequently, a maximal abelian subalgebra within the von Neumann algebra. Our analysis involves characterizing the compact quantum groups whose type functions form a maximal abelian subalgebra, and also identifying those of integer type that are commutative.

Solutions to massive Markov decision problems are often hindered by computational limitations, causing conventional algorithms to become impractically slow. Markov decision problems can be reframemed as linear optimization problems with constraints derived from the Markov process' transition probabilities. This facilitates the application of numerical linear optimization techniques, but the resulting problem still involves infinite-dimensional impracticalities. By employing a cutoff on the problem's nuances, researchers have developed variants of standard linear optimization algorithms, such as the trust region subproblem solver, capable of providing computationally feasible solutions. Building on this work, researchers have refined these algorithms while maintaining their practical advantages, developing a variant of the GMRES algorithm equipped to handle Markov decision problems efficiently. Moreover, researchers have discovered a way to extend the algorithm's applicability to strategies of varying complexity, enhancing its utility. Finally, researchers have devised a method to provide a range of potential solutions rather than a precise one, making the algorithm more resilient to variations in problem data.

Let $D$ be a weighted directed graph and $R$ the ring resulting from its edge ideal. The edge ideal of a weighted directed graph is defined as the ideal in $R$ consisting of all finite formal combinations, with coefficients from the underlying graph's vertices, of directed edges from the graph $D$. In this study, we first determine the conditions under the vertex degree of $R$ equals the sum of its vertices' degrees. Next, we explore the symbolic and normal power series of the edge ideal of a weighted directed graph and we identify the specific parameters under which these power series exhibit a shift in their patterns. Additionally, we provide examples and justify the results with proofs.

Computer simulations that rely on time series data can now be accurately compared with experimental results thanks to the development of a new statistical method. This technique, known as MCE, completes partial derivative equations to accurately represent complex computer simulations, and then uses these representations to estimate model parameters that closely match observed data. When applied to a well-known model in pharmacokinetics, an experimental outcome could be accurately reproduced using only 25 simulations, demonstrating its effectiveness. Additionally, MCE confirmed the reliability of model parameters that were previously assumed to be correct, and revealed the extent of uncertainty associated with another parameter that was previously poorly understood.

Research has demonstrated that local area peers can enhance resilient learning in online settings by mitigating the effects of adversarial attacks. However, the utility of regional queries heavily relies on the quality of the environment distribution and the specifics of the attacker's approach. In this research, we critically examine the conditions under which regional queries can effectively counter attacks from a category of malicious agents known as packet snippers. Our findings indicate that regional queries are capable of protecting against snipers who cut certain packets containing essential data. The safety of regional queries against snipers relying on more sophisticated tactics or those able to target a broader range of packets is unverified.

For the first time, modifications to jet fragmentation in heavy ion collisions have been investigated. Utilizing isolated photons as a trigger, medium-modified proton fragmentation has been examined. Using proton + photon events from the CMS experiment's LHC Run 2 data in PbPb collisions, conclusions can be drawn about the proton's interaction with the Quark-Gluon Plasma. When paired with a high-energy photon, protons are expected to pass through the plasma with minimal alteration, whereas surrounding partons may be influenced. In proton + photon events, changes in charged-particle momentum, collisional loss, and pair production have been assessed across various jet pseudorapidity and transverse momentum thresholds. Observations indicate that, compared to proton-proton collisions, more particles are produced and pair production is increased in the direction of the proton, suggesting that, in addition to cold matter effects, hot matter effects are present. This is particularly evident at higher proton transverse momenta, suggesting a relationship between the proton's energy and the level of interaction with the plasma. These findings may be attributed to the transfer of energy from the QGP to the proton and subsequent showering or, alternatively, an increased availability of groomed particles indicating a more structured proton emergence from the QGP.

Recent research involving the balanced Ap\'{e}ry sequence, a particular type of hypergeometric sequence, found that certain related series could be computed using the Fourier and Jacobi theta functions. This finding was an extension of earlier work presented in papers I and II. The current investigation builds upon this discovery, expressing a distinct sequence, also of a hypergeometric nature, using the modified Chang and Savage identity. The resulting expressions are comprised of three components: the balanced Ap\'{e}ry sequence, an iterated sum of colored harmonic series, and another, distinct sequence, also of a hypergeometric nature. The connection to colored multiple zeta functions becomes apparent when specific constraints are applied to the indices of the harmonic series.

Follow-up research on WISEA J153429.75-104303.3, initially classified as a primary reference for a particular method in photometry, did not yield an in-depth analysis of the object itself. Instead, we found that this object does not fit the expected criteria for the lowest seed temperatures used in the photometric technique called PTI and requires at least three independent data points for accurate calculation, rather than a single measurement as initially proposed. Additionally, we determined that the temperature used in the development of the PTI technique should be at least 150 K rather than 130 K. Our study has also resolved the systematic error of the PTI technique and estimated its upper limit for the temperature error as 40 K, rather than 0.2 K. Furthermore, we defined the criteria for using PTI, such as temperature range, luminosity range, parallax limitations, required data points, and color limitations. Our work has confirmed that WISEA J153429.75-104303.3 is a brown dwarf with an temperature of approximately 550 K and also discussed the object's high proper motion. Finally, we highlighted the challenges and potential issues associated with training machines on astronomical data and recommended steps for addressing these problems.

The ALICE experiment measures the production rates of various particles such as pions, kaons, antiprotons, and phi mesons in Xe-Xe collisions at an energy of 5.44 TeV. These measurements are taken for both mid-rapidity and at several forward rapidities, covering a range of -3 to 3 in mid-rapidity and from $\sqrt{u_{\rm NN}} = 7.68$ GeV to $104.5$ GeV at forward rapidities. The results are then compared to the theoretical Yamaleev model and two Monte Carlo generators: PYTHIA 8 and PHENOMENAL, which are used to quantify how these particle production rates vary depending on factors like whether an event includes central or peripheral collisions, and how much energy is transferred in each collision.

In this work, the evolution of parton distribution functions and their accuracy are examined with particular focus on how quickly NNLO (two-loop) DGLAP corrections converge towards NLO (one-loop) results as evolution deepens goes. Employing the Z-boson fragmentation function as a test case, our analysis reveals that, for small x, NLO and NNLO DGLAP series differ by a factor of at least 1000 even at x as low as 10^-6. This finding is further supported by the fact that, in a pre-LLAPD framework, all four-parton contributions to the fragmentation function come from the region x < 10^-4. Our results suggest the necessity of incorporating at least NNLO corrections to accurately describe parton distribution functions, especially in the region where x is very small.

Specimens made of Martian and Lunar soil substitutes were created in a press and heated in an electric furnace to examine their internal structure and resistance after being exposed to different heating processes. The internal structure and strength of these materials were analyzed under various thermal conditions to determine how they vary. The findings show that the internal structure and strength of these materials vary significantly based on the heating temperature. The formation of a dense and crystal-bound structure occurs at lower temperatures (around 250-300 degrees Celsius), whereas a porous and metal-rich structure forms at higher temperatures (above 1000 degrees Celsius). To construct infrastructure on Mars and the Moon, it's essential to understand how the native soil substitutes react to different temperatures to predict their behavior in environmental structures.

The Rayleigh-Plateau instability occurs when a liquid layer on a cylindrical substrate undergoes spherical cap instability, causing the liquid to form droplets on the substrate. However, this process can be influenced significantly if the liquid layer on the fiber is not perfectly attached, exhibiting slip. By incorporating this slip factor into the model, the theoretical framework has been modified. Consequently, the linear stability analysis reveals that liquid layers with zero slip and pure non-attached layers exhibit identical stability characteristics, whereas an intermediate level of slip exists within a specific numerical range. Furthermore, the influence of slip on growth rates becomes linear and inversely proportional to the slip coefficient. Notably, when the liquid and cylinder surfaces have identical material properties, the effect of slip is maximal.

By comparing observed and predicted data, the accuracy of SED-fitting models for estimating star formation rates is assessed. On average, the SED models tend to underestimate these rates by about 25 percent when using a line of interest and by about 15 percent when using other methods. However, there is notable variation in these discrepancies. By adjusting the parameters of the models used, the deviation from the observed data can be minimized. Ultimately, the choice of methods to use depends on the goals of the research and whether prioritizing the utilization of certain diagnostic lines or the creation of photometric tables is more important.

This is the initial paper in a two-part series aimed at categorizing a substantial number of the type II quantum subgroups within the specified categories $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$. In this particular study, we establish the symmetries existing between regional modules within the categories under discussion, which are linked to the quantum subgroups of interest. These regional modules correspond to parallel weight modules that contain significant elements of the FSL$(N,k)$ group. These elements form a substantial subset of the type II quantum subgroups. Notably, the regional modules associated with duals of the fundamental modules hold substantial importance as their central objects. In the follow-up to this paper, we will apply the findings presented here to thoroughly classify all the type II quantum subgroups within the specified categories $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$.

Diffusion processes play a crucial role in scientific disciplines such as biology, physics and chemistry, and their applications extend to mark forecasting, state transportation and data generation. Fuglekvam et al. introduced the universal heat equation from a probabilistic perspective in 2021, and it has since been expanded into a comprehensive framework for universal diffusion. This paper presents a groundbreaking method to generate solutions for the universal heat equation, enabling the production of marked paths compatible with both Brownian and Poisson laws without requiring auxiliary variables or approximations. This new method offers impressive computational efficiency, allowing for the creation of millions of marked paths in just milliseconds. Additionally, we demonstrate the ability to obtain solutions for any given time $t$ in $O(N)$ time, exceeding the $O(N^{1/4})$ time achieved through Monte Carlo simulations. This paper also explores the universal convection-diffusion equation, revealing that existing solutions may be flawed due to an incorrect forward equation. A practical use of the universal diffusion is demonstrated in forecasting the trajectory of a human using a hidden state model.

This research outlines a method to recognize handwritten mathematical expressions using multi-touch device data. Our approach involves analyzing the sequence of touch events to determine the expression's structure, and then using a dictionary-based word recognition technique to identify the mathematical operators and symbols within the expression. The validity of our approach was tested through a case study involving a system called AirMath, and our analysis shows that it is able to accurately recognize a wide variety of mathematical expressions across different domains, with a low error rate. Furthermore, our evaluation demonstrates that this method is capable of functioning effectively even in the presence of a minimal footprint and limited processing capabilities, making it a feasible solution for mobile, resource-constrained systems that require mathematical expression recognition.

This research develops an innovative, token-level approach to forming sentences of varied lengths for pre-training language models, as existing methods using probabilistic sentences are constrained by limitations. The proposed method, centered on medians, creates two diverse sentence extensions through either insertion or deletion of words, ensuring compatibility with the existing vocabulary. The approach is further refined through analysis of synthetic and genuine sentence pairs. This method enjoys advantages including low computational requirements, a full vocabulary, and adaptability to various languages. It yields substantial enhancements in zero-shot speech-to-text evaluation metrics and establishes a foundation for developing more sophisticated sentence generation techniques.

Species distribution analysis can be effectively conducted through occupancy modeling, taking into consideration inaccuracies in species detection data. To address multiple species, states, interactions, imputation methods, and spatial correlations can be incorporated. Our research introduces spOccupancy for building and evaluating various occupancy models, utilizing Bayesian approaches to bridge theoretical and practical considerations. The package includes essential tools like model formula construction, prior distribution selection, compilation, evaluation, and comparison. It also facilitates simulation, unit testing, and data visualization tasks.

The Skincare initiative, a interactive deep learning system, has been designed to identify and characterize skin cancers that exhibit unique properties. This report outlines the technical framework and showcases the performance of the Skincare initiative, which comprises a series of neural networks that analyze imaging data and clinical information to differentiate various types of skin cancers. The Skincare initiative's performance and stability are evaluated through numerous clinical studies, demonstrating its ability to characterize malignant skin lesions reliably. This technical framework can be adapted to support skin cancer diagnosis and treatment, with potential applications in clinical settings and research initiatives.

To improve the modeling of Type Ia supernovae temporal series data, we developed a customized flow-based autoencoder. This method treats time as a continuous variable and leverages its inherent property to inform the data generation process. By incorporating a stochastic step in the encoding process, we enable the removal of arbitrary scaling and shifting in the latent space, effectively disentangling latent factors. Our approach employs a mixture model modulated by latent variables to account for grouping within the data and handles censored values by using a soft max function. We evaluate the effectiveness of our model through various diagnostic tools, such as the comparison of marginals and pair-wise dependencies between observed and reconstructed values. Furthermore, we utilize our model to extract features and assess the model's ability to reproduce the original data distribution by evaluating its goodness-of-fit with a diverse set of models. Our model offers a general framework that can be applied to other temporal series data.

A large-scale gravitational lensing by a massive galaxy at z = 2.09 has been discovered in a Distant Light survey, revealing a massive molecular cloud with a massive dust nucleus forming a star. For the first time, researchers have directly observed the escape of neutral gas from a galaxy with an active star-forming core, which is the initial phase of galaxy formation. By analyzing the cloud's properties, it is estimated that the galaxy would have formed a massive, diffuse nebula if the dust had not been present. It is also possible that similar clouds contributed to the formation of galaxies that existed in the early universe.

We experimentally investigate how solid particles behave when moving up through
a turbulent water column that's being stirred from the bottom. The turbulence in
this scenario is caused by a heat source at the base that produces a plume with
incorporating particles rising through it. The characteristics of the particles,
such as size and density, greatly affect how they interact with the plume. For
particles with a low density relative to the surrounding fluid, but a medium or
large size, the plume becomes narrower and its top moves slower than it would
without particles. This is because the particles move downward into the steepest
parts of the plume, limiting its expansion. Even dense particles have a similar
effect on the plume but their impact is less pronounced. The particles' motion
into the steepest parts of the plume can be described using a theoretical model and
this description matches our experimental findings well.

For complex networks that use hyperedges to connect groups of interested individuals to topics, like viruses or infectious ideologies, we create a model that predicts the outcome of an epidemic spread. Focusing on the intrinsic properties of the network and disregarding disease specifics, our framework allows the determination of critical thresholds beyond which epidemics inevitably occur, regardless of initial infection conditions. To investigate these critical thresholds, we develop two theorems: the First, which applies to networks composed of trees and specifies upper and lower bounds for the threshold; and the Second, applicable to all networks, which determines the threshold by maximizing a spectral parameter over the space of positive semidefinite matrices. Related theories for the intrinsic properties of networks are also discussed.

The Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction's contribution to the spin profile in the bilayer of the 2D ferromagnet chromium iodide has been investigated through a combined study of its magnetic properties and the symmetry of its crystal structure. By considering the effects of symmetry-allowed and symmetry-forbidden Rashba states at the interface of the bilayer, the required symmetry properties are clarified for the generation of a chiral magnetic phase. Additionally, the formation of an in-plane spin helix in the bilayer is discussed in relation to the symmetry of its magnetic domains.

Investigating potential magnetic cycles in slowly rotating stars is crucial. We conducted extensive simulations of solar-type dynamos, allowing for variations in rotation rate, magnetic pruning, and thermal and magnetic boundary conditions. To account for the Sun's distinctive anti-solar polynomial differential rotation, we used Babcock-Leighton flux-transport models, while adjusting parameters to mimic the Sun's rotational profile. Our results indicate that strong magnetic cycles are only achievable if the acceleration of the rotational shearing instability and magnetic pruning are equally robust. Slow rotation prevents magnetic cycles from occurring, with even slightly weak pruning preventing the buildup of global magnetic fields. We observed that moderate quasi-steady magnetic fields can persist in slowly rotating stars with efficient magnetic pruning, suggesting possible mean-field $\alpha$-effects even in the absence of cyclic magnetism. These findings may have implications for the global geometry of magnetic fields in slowly rotating stars.

Deep learning models can process multiple input streams, such as text, images, and tabs, but currently available models are either complex or inefficient, often requiring separate networks for each input type and/or not leveraging the strength of shared representations. Our new model, the K-fan deep learning framework, addresses these issues by allowing simultaneous processing of up to five input streams through a shared transformation network, and enabling the use of shared information across different inputs by means of connections. Our model can easily be adapted to fit various tasks by incorporating additional control modules and loss functions. Moreover, using shared information as input to the control module reduces the risk of overfitting. When tested on three distinct tasks - extracting semantic information from text and images, state tracking in tables, and generating summaries based on multiple inputs - our model outperformed existing task-specific models and other deep learning models designed for multiple inputs. Our results also show that using shared representations can improve performance by up to 25% over models without this feature. Overall, the K-fan model is a versatile and efficient tool for processing multiple input streams in a task-related manner, and its success may vary depending on the specific application at hand.

McMini, a static model verifier for multithreaded programs, uses a abstract machine to determine if a program's executions conform to a specified program model that ensures correct functionality. The abstract machine applies a DPOR (Distributed Past Object Reference) algorithm to perform reachability analysis and determines a control flow relation between program threads. The relationship is used to calculate an abstract distance between program states, enabling McMini to determine if a program state is reachable. The model's validity includes thread synchronization mechanisms, such as locks, and safety properties defined over program models. McMini is compatible with McMillan's mini model checker and supports abstract representations of program states and control flow graphs. It provides incremental reasoning with thread subsets, and its source code is freely accessible on GitHub.

The widespread circulation of false information is exacerbated by messaging apps allowing users to share content with large groups of people, and WhatsApp has become a key platform for spreading misinformation due to its vast user base and encryption, which protects users' conversations. In response to the issue, WhatsApp introduced a feature limiting the number of people users can directly message to 8, and an option to report misleading information to friends or groups. However, concerns remain over the app's ability to effectively address the problem. Our study aims to evaluate the impact of these features by examining user behavior, particularly sending and receiving messages, before and after the changes, and measuring the effect on misinformation dissemination. Our analysis reveals that users adhere to the new limitations, leading to significant reductions in activity, and an average decline of 70% in received messages. Interestingly, the modification appears to have had little influence on the spread of false information, suggesting that groups play a crucial role in misinformation dissemination. Users frequently share set pieces of content, and most misinformation is distributed within private chats rather than public groups. As a result, targeting public groups alone may be insufficient in combating the issue.

The frequency distribution of alleles in populations that experience branching growth,
unaffected by the size of individual families, resembles the distribution seen in populations
that experience branching growth with varying family sizes, although the latter is influenced
by family size parameters. This conclusion is based on the comparison of the mean and
variance of allele frequencies in both types of populations. Specifically, the second moment
of allele frequencies in populations that experience branching growth is proportional to the
branching ratio raised to the power of three, while being independent of family size
parameters. This finding is supported through simulations under a specific model of new mutations.

Current deep neural network-based systems used to differentiate genuine and fake voice recordings often overlook the details in their activation functions, which can provide valuable information in distinguishing between real and fake voices. By utilizing a custom-made Vigilant activation function, we enhance the capabilities of current systems to counteract voice spoofing. This function achieves its effectiveness by balancing the model's bias and weight adjustments in accordance with the system's output feedback. Furthermore, it maintains data normalization by adjusting the scale of output gradients. Following thorough analysis, our proposed system was successfully tested on the Interspeech 2019 challenge dataset and demonstrated improved performance in classifying real and fake voices.

Supergravity, being a subset of string theory, offers an attractive framework 
for studying inflationary field theories due to their inherent constraints on 
physical properties. Theoretical completeness in supergravity implies that any 
reliable quantum field theory can be formulated within this framework, making 
it an indispensable tool for researchers. Our study examines the dynamics of 
scalar fields in locally supersymmetric theories, applying an efficient 
parametrization that simplifies complex Kähler potential and holomorphic 
prepotentials. These generalise previous works to a broader range of models, 
enabling us to investigate cosmological dynamics of diverse field theories, 
including multiple examples with substantial interest. These examples encompass 
models of two-field dependence, power-law inflation, $\aleph$-attractor models, 
and $A$-model inflation. Our findings provide quantum field theory 
characterisations, specifying scaling relations, power spectra, and spectral 
indices for each example, thereby facilitating comparison with cosmic 
observations. Our results also cover reheating phases in supergravity models, 
attesting to the efficacy of this framework in guiding quantum field theory.

The standard model describes nonphoton processes at a particle accelerator's collision point, but reveals discrepancies with experimental data in photon pair correlations. We argue that asymmetry in photon polarization should be considered a possible explanation for these discrepancies. Our proposal includes two experimental tests: one to observe left-right asymmetry by adjusting the angle between the photons and another to observe forward-backward asymmetry by adjusting the collision point's distance from the photon production point. If a notable effect is observed at existing experiments, it's likely that asymmetry causes the standard model's discrepancies. Also, if observed, this phenomenon could be studied to determine the dialion's mass. Ultimately, a more precise measurement of the dialion's mass could be made at a future experiment specifically designed to observe the dialion's influence on photon pair correlations.

THz surface wave detectors made from high-mobility semiconductor materials can significantly enhance sensitivity in quantum research. We are seeing growing interest in utilizing these detectors for purposes such as nondestructive characterization of quantum devices and measurement of entanglement in systems involving a large number of qubits. To increase the effectiveness of these detectors, it is crucial to gain a deeper understanding of their microscopic properties, especially when they are used in near-field terahertz scanning applications. We have conducted near-field terahertz nanoscopy of planar microwave resonators and were able to provide a detailed analysis of their microscopic properties, revealing defects in the materials and microshunts in electromagnetic circuits. Our research demonstrates the potential of THz nanoscale detection as a powerful tool for investigating the physical properties of quantum systems and discovering their inherent characteristics.

We are looking for the highest cardinality of subsets divided by Borel measurements, covering the real line from $-\beta$ to $\beta$, given a fixed Borel measure. This problem was first proposed by Borel himself in 1972 and our study determines the upper limit for this cardinality under two different scenarios: when the real line is partitioned into countable subsets of intervals or non-empty sets, respectively. Our research yields upper bounds that are independent of the chosen partition method, but exceed those derived from previous studies on dividing the real line into countable subsets. Furthermore, we present an example of a measure, specifically the Lebesgue measure, where the upper limit for this cardinality exceeds any finite value.

This study examines the impact of novel investment tactics on existing strategies in a simulated environment. Our analysis involves four novel tactics and six established strategies, with our agent-based model simulating a financial market with multiple agents. Our results indicate that novel tactics can either enhance existing strategies or suppress them, depending on the characteristics of the tactics and the market conditions. Our findings also suggest that novel tactics may exacerbate the performance disparity in certain situations, but our research does not support the hypothesis that novel tactics necessarily undermine existing strategies. Instead, the outcomes are influenced by complex interactions between the novel tactics, the existing strategies, and market conditions.

A growing number of network security monitoring systems rely on passive deep packet inspection to analyze network traffic patterns and prevent or respond to threats. Some systems use a combination of multiple identification methods, while others solely rely on deep packet inspection, making them more susceptible to spoofing. This study focuses on identifying and mitigating assault vectors that can deceive passive deep packet inspection-based systems, potentially causing false positives or security system overload. Two new assault vectors were developed, one of which targets SSL/TLS and another that targets HTTP-based systems, allowing for a comprehensive analysis and evaluation of their effectiveness.

The integration of superconducting proximate materials into magnonic circuits holds great promise for generating and controlling quantum states within these systems. To achieve this, it is crucial to understand how the interaction between superconducting spins and nearby magnons functions as a means of filtering out unwanted frequency ranges. By applying a combination of numerical techniques and analytical modeling, we investigate the efficiency of a superconducting-induced barrier in regulating the flow of magnons. Our results indicate that this barrier effectively prevents low-frequency magnons from passing through while allowing higher-frequency magnons to pass. Additionally, we found that the direction of the superconducting spin's spin-polarization exerts a significant impact on the magnon's transmission probability. Therefore, the precise control of the spin-polarization in proximate superconductors offers a potential means of manipulating and filtering magnonic signals.

A significant challenge in machine learning lies in efficiently handling the practical limitations of data availability, computational resources, and model complexity. Our research tackles this problem by developing a distributed, zero-shot learning approach for audio classification tasks. Unlike typical scenarios where model fine-tuning is feasible, our method enables outstanding performance without necessitating data, parameters, or labels from novel classes. Our experiment on the SCOPUS database showcases the effectiveness of our solution.

Creating high-dimensional complex quantum systems like the Greenberger-Horne-Zeilberg state demands significant experimental resources but often yields limited understanding of the resulting state. We have developed a theoretical framework to analyze and verify the formation of the GHZ state in n-qubit systems using stochastic trilinear forms. This method allows for determining the degree of entanglement among particles and detecting deviations from the desired state in case of errors. Our proposal is applied to optical realizations of GHZ states in various systems, demonstrating that measuring eigenfunctions of certain operators can help experimentally determine the performance of these experiments.

To efficiently utilize scarce wireless communication bandwidth, Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS)-assisted communication systems have gained attention for creating intelligent and resource-efficient networks. However, rapid changes in the channels and high computational complexity associated with real-time IRS beamforming have hindered large-scale deployment. We address these challenges by implementing a novel cascaded channel assessment approach for multi-user multiple-input-single-output (MISO) systems. This approach utilizes deep learning (DL) to simplify the complex channel assessment problem, reducing computational complexity and enabling real-time optimization. Furthermore, we leverage a batch sparsification technique to minimize memory requirements and speed up training, making it suitable for large-scale network applications. Our numerical results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach in achieving a balance between energy efficiency and channel assessment accuracy.

The COVID-19 pandemic has led to significant mortality and economic disruption worldwide. News coverage plays a crucial role in informing the public and shaping community responses, with regional variations in reporting contributing to public fear and behavior. We examined online news from 312 U.S. regions over a 22-month period, analyzing the relationship between regional COVID news, cases and deaths, and demographics. Notably, areas with more traumatic news coverage experienced higher COVID death rates and attracted populations prone to stress. Conversely, areas with more informational coverage experienced lower COVID death rates and attracted populations seeking knowledge. Our findings highlight the influence of regional news styles on COVID outcomes, stressing the need for journalists to balance both persuasive and informative goals.

Human counting abilities advance significantly with experience, yet the intricate relationship between practice and expertise remains poorly understood. To uncover the key factors contributing to counting proficiency, we developed and tested a neural network model that incorporates short-term and long-term memory mechanisms. The network's design, which builds upon the MONET model, features adjustable parameters for modeling the influence of practice, expertise, and memory on counting performance. We validated the model by validating a previously proposed counting paradigm, which indicates that counting ability improves through cumulative experience. Additionally, our model suggests that memory plays a significant role in distinguishing between expert and novice counters.

Bloom filters provide fast approximations of set membership while consuming minimal memory. However, they suffer from inaccurate predictions and wasted space due to unnecessary false positives. In contrast, cuckoo filters offer more accurate results at similar memory costs by utilizing fully associative arrays and incorporating data structures like hash tables. Notwithstanding this, they still experience false positives and waste space.

This research introduces XOR filters, a new family of approximate membership filters that outperform both Bloom and cuckoo filters. XOR filters operate by storing sets via hash-based mapping of elements to fixed-length binary sequences, which are then combined to form a compact, full-hash-tray proxy of the original set. They leverage the properties of hash functions to guarantee a high probability of accurate predictions, also ensuring that false positives do not occur in pairs. This property enables more efficient garbage collection and thus reduces memory waste and the need for space estimation.

Experiments were conducted to compare the performance of XOR filters against industry-standard Bloom and cuckoo filters. Results showed XOR filters outperform these alternatives in both accuracy and efficiency, often remarkably so in specific scenarios. For example, they typically require less than half the memory needed by Bloom filters while providing nearly equivalent prediction accuracy. Similarly, they need around 30% of the memory needed by cuckoo filters while offering much higher prediction accuracy.

XOR filters have already been successfully integrated into etcd, a distributed key-value storage system, demonstrating their practicality and potential for broader applications.

This brief note showcases connections between various concepts in convex topology and those in complex geometry, specifically K-stability and presence of canonical metrics. The relationships demonstrated are based on the following premises: the Euler-Satake characteristic of pairs $(X,D)$ and $(X',D')$ are equivalent if they share topological equivalents; the completion of the space of effective divisors on $X$ with the Lipschitz topology is equivalent to the space of K-stable pairs on $X$. These premises are proven by combining two facts: an argument based on the concept of mixed Hodge pairs for-every Delzant polytope, and the established result that if a divisor is smoothly convergent within a K-stable pair, then it forms a mixed Hodge pair.

A new approach to analyze market trends is presented, relying solely on sequences of transaction data, disregarding other information. This methodology separates the trading interval into three distinct segments: past, present, and future. The 'past' segment contains consecutive transactions leading up to the current time, while the 'future' segment comprises subsequent transactions that occur after the current time, and the 'present' segment consists of a single transaction, representing the current trade. Our analysis focuses on how the 'future' segment's trends are impacted by the 'past' segment's trends, where a trend in the 'past' segment is established by calculating the price difference relative to the number of transactions, and then applying this ratio to a set of future transaction counts. Several simulation tests using historical NYSE data confirm that the presence of a trend in the 'past' segment increases the likelihood of similar trends in the 'future' segment, and even predicts trends in the 'present' segment. Our study adopts the conservative conditions of Bocquet, where the 'past' segment contains 10 consecutive transactions, and the 'future' segment comprises 50 subsequent transactions, and also includes 50 consecutive transactions that serve as a reference. Our analysis reveals that the reference trends closely match the trends derived from the sequences in the 'future' segment, demonstrating the efficacy of this approach in predicting market trends.

The rapid growth in machine learning (ML) is significantly influenced by the techniques known as data augmentation and mixture-of-experts (MoE). Despite the efficiency of these methods, they come with drawbacks: a need for extensive labeled data and non-parallel training and inference processes, respectively. Federated learning (FL) has been proposed as an effective way to address these issues by allowing the training of ML models in distributed settings. However, current FL implementations are unable to support data augmentation or MoE architectures due to efficiency and privacy concerns. To bridge this gap, we present FLVoogd, a novel federated learning framework that can efficiently train state-of-the-art ML models while protecting users' privacy and maintaining computational efficiency. The framework leverages techniques such as local data shaping, group-based training, and secure binary aggregations to create a robust FL solution. The efficacy of FLVoogd is tested on various data augmentation and MoE models, and it demonstrates significant training speed and test accuracy improvements over existing approaches.

The ultimate goal of autonomous vehicle development is to seamlessly transition from simulated environments to real-world settings, yet current methods fall short of achieving a direct translation. This paper bridges the Sim2Real gap by utilizing gradient information from images to establish a consistent framework for autonomous navigation. By employing a consistent representation, we can leverage previously collected data to train autonomous navigation models, thereby eliminating the need for extensive real-world data collection. To achieve this, we developed a novel method that extracts a consistent gridded representation from both simulated and real-world settings, based on the inherent structure of streets and navigation pathways. This representation is then applied to estimate a consistent grid map, which serves as a unified representation for navigation. Ultimately, this approach enables autonomous navigation models to directly utilize data collected from simulations to inform real-world driving. Our experimental findings, based on various benchmarks, consistently demonstrate a substantial improvement in performance on real-world vehicles, quantified as a 6.44% reduction in collision frequency and a $230 reduction in scanning frequency.

Significant progress in deep learning technology has enabled the creation of more convincingly authentic deepfakes, which have sparked interest across multiple sectors due to their vast potential applications, despite raising serious societal and security risks. This chapter provides an overview of the development and prevention techniques for deepfakes, covering state-of-the-art methods in deepfake creation and detection, as well as innovative high-risk, high-reward approaches in this field.

The composition of exoplanets known as sub-Neptunes is largely unknown, with most featuring similar mass and size. It has been proposed that these planets have solid cores and H/He atmospheres, but this is purely speculative. A new approach is proposed, using transmissions spectra to distinguish between liquid and gaseous components, focusing on the internal structures of these planets. By analyzing the internal structures of mock terrestrial planets with oceans and H/He atmospheres, it is possible to model the transmission spectra. The proposed method can differentiate between various liquid and gaseous components and is not limited to H/Ne atmospheres. Additionally, it is possible to model the thermal history of these planets and their internal structures. The proposed method is expected to be effective in detecting small amounts of volatile elements in sub-Neptunes and identifying oceans within these planets, thus expanding our understanding of their internal structures.

Inspired by biological neurons, spiking neural networks have the potential to replace traditional neural networks, despite their complex learning dynamics. A significant hurdle has been the lack of an efficient learning algorithm, but recent breakthroughs include modified backpropagation and gradient descent methods. However, these adaptations still raise conceptual difficulties. Our work addresses this challenge by developing a learning protocol grounded in bio-plausibility, informed by metabolic constraints. Unlike existing learning algorithms, our approach doesn't rely on continuous weight updates or elaborate memory mechanisms. Instead, we utilize local, short-term synaptic changes and leverage the network's structural properties, as well as the temporal dynamics of spike sequences. We illustrate the efficacy of our protocol, called Synaptic Learning Rule, through simulations of binary and graded-spike neurons, and show that it compares favorably to existing methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency.

This report outlines the results of the out-of-context (ooc) challenge, an essential task in conversational AI, where models are tested on their ability to understand dialogue snippets outside of their original context. The ooc challenge was included in the third conversation evaluation challenge (CONVKT-3), which provided benchmarks for assessing conversation models in ooc and multi-turn scenarios. The ooc challenge comprised three sub-tasks: to classify whether a sentence is within or outside of its context, to identify the speaker of a sentence, and to determine the sentence's role in a conversation. The classification task revealed a significant gap between leading conversation models and a strong non-language model baseline in the out-of-context classification task, with similar findings observed in the speaker identification task. However, a strong language model baseline performed competitively in the ooc classification task. The report discusses potential improvements to the ooc dataset and the challenge, including the use of more comprehensive datasets, more accurate task definitions, and stricter evaluation methods. Furthermore, the report notes that addressing the ooc challenge may require a multi-faceted approach involving both methodological and linguistic advancements.

A specific type of generalized polynomial chaos expansion is verified in this study. The verification process involves establishing an error bound that can be controlled. Existing error analysis in various contexts relies on statistical properties of the differential operator involved, but these results fall short for crucial cases. For example, verification is impossible for partial differential equations with chaotic parameters. To address this shortcoming, a novel approach utilizing an iterative process is proposed. This approach, however, introduces an unappealing aspect - it imposes extremely strict restrictions on the smoothness of the solution function. In an effort to overcome this obstacle, a iterative process is proposed, allowing a degree of instability in exchange for improved smoothness. Although this approach is explored primarily with regression in mind, it is also applicable to partial differential equations.

To effectively monitor and detect deviations in adaptable systems with varied patterns, such as those found in cyber-physical systems, we need to identify and isolate abnormalities in real-time. However, due to constraints like limited resources and complex architectures, it's often impossible to obtain complete and precise data. Therefore, we've developed a new adaptive approach that can identify and isolate abnormalities in real-time, even with imperfect observations. Our approach employs model-agnostic techniques, allowing it to be widely applied across various cyber-physical systems that exhibit piecewise linear behavior. To resolve the computational challenges, we've developed an efficient and progressive algorithm that utilizes the concept of Viterbi decoding, allowing it to run in real-time and efficiently tackle large-scale systems with complex patterns. Additionally, we've devised a graphical representation to visually understand and validate the performance of our approach, even near its performance limits. Through case studies and simulations, we've verified that our approach outperforms existing methods by a significant margin - up to 30% improvement. Furthermore, we've demonstrated that our approach's performance gains are substantial, with up to  Born to Risk: 5.75 vs 8.15 (our approach's average number of false alarms per hour vs existing methods' average number of false alarms per hour).

A comprehensive analysis of basic characteristics, star formation histories, and metal content in a sample of 232 dwarf galaxies has enabled further subcategorization of the dwarf galaxy population. This population has been divided into six distinct subtypes, namely, Late-Type Dwarf galaxies, their pseudo-early counterparts, and four separate Early-Type Dwarf galaxy subtypes, which exhibit distinct evolutionary patterns. The presence of the Milky Way's satellite galaxies primarily drives this classification. Conversely, differences in the galactic environment are responsible for the varying chemical compositions and star formation histories within each subtype, whereas the initial mass of these dwarf galaxies determines their respective metal content levels. The discovery of mass-dependent star formation patterns in dwarf galaxies presents an opportunity to apply feedback mechanisms in numerical simulations to understand the galactic evolution process, which could lead to the development of proto-galactic cores. This, in turn, may influence the formation of the galactic halo and its subsequent interaction with the galactic disk.

We define a homotopy action spectrum as an intrinsic, profinite group-based space that emerges from the continuous orbit graph of an action, incorporating unstable homotopy classes and establishing a connection with finite homotopy action spectra. By doing so, we obtain a straightforward method for constructing a profinite group-based homotopy classification of finite CW-complexes, and this result is combined with previous research to provide a profinite group-based classification of finite CW-complexes up to homotopy, characterized solely by their homotopy groups.

The cost of training advanced machine learning models to extract insights from complex documents is typically restricted by the expense of gathering a substantial number of labeled examples. In this research, we present a pioneering approach that efficiently utilizes a small number of labeled samples to accurately classify and extract data from a wide variety of documents. By combining low-level visual features with pre-trained natural language models and prioritizing areas of the document that require more training examples to be annotated, we effectively concentrate the model's attention on sections that can easily be identified. This simple yet effective technique allows us to achieve superior levels of accuracy in data extraction, surpassing current state-of-the-art models that require a vast number of labeled samples. We test our approach by extracting information from invoices, which are typically visually rich and diverse. Given the limitations inherent to optical character recognition technology, we found that a relatively small number of labeled examples are required to achieve high levels of accuracy in this task. The model's performance is evaluated using both supervised and semi-supervised evaluation metrics, providing insight into the effectiveness of this approach in practical scenarios.

The EuS/InAs interface electronic structure varies depending on the bonding configuration. There are two possible arrangements of the interface, which are anti-Frenkel and common bond dispositions. The common bond disposition exhibits a 0-eV energy range in the density of states, indicating significant charge localization. In contrast, the anti-Frenkel disposition lacks this 0-eV energy range. The charge localized at the common bond disposition interface arises from the spin-polarized Eu 5d states and InAs 5s states of the EuS/InAs interface. The calculated magnetic properties are consistent with experimental findings. The time-of-flight mobility, Hall resistance, and magnetoresistance all indicate a common bond configuration at the EuS/InAs interface.

A fundamental concept in continuous logic revolves around Borel Wadge classes, which are used to group continuous Boolean formulas according to their assigned Borel degrees of complexity. Tracing back to John Myhill's work from 1958, an efficient method for categorizing these classes has yet to be established. We address this issue by designing an efficient procedure that assigns each Borel Wadge class a unique code, consisting of a finite sequence of fundamental priorities, and develops an algorithm enabling efficient determination of the Borel degree of any given continuous formula. This code-cataloging system has a key property: it retains consistency under any subsequent expansions of the underlying continuous theory. We demonstrate that our codes continue to convey meaningful information about the complexity of the associated formulas, even when the underlying theory is expanded. Specifically, we show that our codes still pick out distinct subsets within Borel space, even in the presence of additional assumptions. Furthermore, we keep the length of the code sequences resulting from this procedure relatively short - the maximum code sequence has a length of 32. This efficiency builds upon prior work by Allen in which code sequences of a length of 16 were used.

Deep, wide, and complex Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are increasingly preferred, but efficient training on them is a significant challenge. Although techniques like quantization and pruning can facilitate this, most existing methods involve retraining the model after pruning which results in poor final model accuracy. There's a trade-off between the amount of pruning (throughout the training process) and the amount of retraining needed (after the model is developed), both of which affect end-to-end deep learning training efficiency. A new approach called ClickTrain is proposed, which allows for precise and effective end-to-end deep learning training by allowing architecture-preserving pruning throughout the training process without requiring retraining. This involves analyzing the weight changes and making adjustments accordingly, with a strategy for handling uncertainties during model computation. ClickTrain is compared with other methods like DDP and FP16 through various experiments on ResNet-46 models, with results showing it can reduce the memory usage and computational requirements by up to 81 times without compromising the final model's accuracy.

This research examines the full expressive power of the Distributive Complete Lambek Calculus with Modal Functions (dCLMF). We first demonstrate that dCLMF is equivalently represented by structured logics based on the categorical framework of structured bilinearity and also by the existing Kameya-Nakanishi extension of Prawitz's original expansion of the Lambek calculus.

The collisions of neutron star-black hole mergers yield diverse signals across various gravitational wave detectors, spanning multiple science fields, including nuclear physics, astrophysics, and component population studies. Signal duration and morphology greatly vary, posing significant challenges for the identification and classification of these events, particularly through reliance on sparse and noisy data from a single detector. To overcome these obstacles, researchers have developed an artificial neural network (ANN) called FastClass, capable of accurately detecting and classifying mergers in real-time, even when data is restricted to a single detector signal. By utilizing a compact network design with an inherent timescale, FastClass is able to identify collisions across the entire neutron star-black hole spectrum, while its symmetric structure allows it to perform rotations-free, a key advantage. Furthermore, the network's structure is simplified by the incorporation of constrained parameters, such as mass ratios and spin parameters, and is not subject to overfitting. Through comparison with the standard GWFAST algorithm, researchers have shown that FastClass is capable of identifying approximately 90% of detectable collisions, with high accuracy in mass ratio and spin parameter estimates, particularly when data from multiple detectors is available. However, the network's performance begins to break down for the rarest and weakest collisions. Ultimately, the integration of FastClass into the LIGO-Virgo pipeline will greatly enhance the discovery of neutron star-black hole mergers, significantly expanding the range of science that these gravitational wave events will enable.

A new discovery has been made regarding a gas giant exoplanet, which is one of the oldest found so far. The researchers have identified the exoplanet, which is called TOI-5542 b, using data from the TESS satellite mission. TOI-5542 b is a hot Jupiter-sized planet that orbits its host star at an extremely close distance, which takes approximately 3.17 days. The interesting aspect of this exoplanet is that it is composed mainly of gas, which is a rare characteristic of planets orbiting G-dwarf stars, which typically have higher levels of metal content. The discovery of TOI-5542 b adds to the existing list of old exoplanets, which are those detected around older host stars. Old exoplanets are of great significance to scientists, as they provide valuable insights into the processes that shape the formation and evolution of planetary systems. The presence of hot Jupiters, which are gas-giant exoplanets orbiting close to their host stars, is particularly significant, as they are considered to require planetary migration, which is a theoretical mechanism that explains the origin of these planets. The researchers used data from follow-up studies, which included spectrography and transit photometry. The resulting data confirmed the existence of TOI-5542 b and provided more accurate details about its mass and composition. The study found that TOI-5542 d, which is another exoplanet detected in the same planetary system,

Markov decision processes (MDPs) form the foundation of many models that incorporate temporal considerations, such as dynamic preference models and explanations for serial order. In some scenarios, it is beneficial to impose preferences that adhere to certain rules, but these restrictions may not be sufficient to eliminate all issues with preference elicitation. To address the resulting complication, researchers often employ the concept of Markov choice procedures (MCPs), which involve using state sequences or other temporal structures to guide choice procedures that take account of time. These methods can be viewed as generalizations of both MDPs and preference models that incorporate temporal elements, as well as other theories such as temporal choice models. To address the issue of validating preferences that adhere to certain rules, researchers have developed methods such as finding the closest "admissible" preference relation to the respondent's actual preferences. These algorithms are motivated by the idea that restricting the set of admissible preferences may help to eliminate inconsistencies, and can be seen as a form of regularization. To develop these methods, researchers have formulated the task as a linear programming problem, and demonstrated that they are equivalent to finding an optimal solution to a dual problem from a convex optimization problem, and provide x% approximation guarantees when solved to $(1-x)$% accuracy. This paper presents an efficient primal-dual method for solving these problems, and demonstrates that it achieves similar results with only slightly higher computational requirements. Mathematical notation handwriting recognition is a complex and diverse challenge
due to the wide range of mathematical symbols and expressions that must be
recognized. Traditional approaches have focused on using context-dependent features and
probabilistic frameworks for analysis. Recent advancements in deep learning have
enabled the development of new strategies, which are also discussed in this study.
Our proposed method utilizes a deep neural network-based architecture for recognizing
mathematical notation. The approach has been tested using a substantial dataset of
mathematical expressions and evaluated in terms of accuracy across various writing
styles and speeds. Our work has been successful in achieving high levels of accuracy
and demonstrating the potential of deep learning for handling complex recognition
tasks.

A geometric interpretation is provided for superconformal quantum mechanics based on a hyper-Kahler cone that has supersymmetric BPS states. It's demonstrated that BPS state energies form a grid, where each point corresponds to a specific supersymmetric quantum mechanics eigenvalue. Furthermore, it's shown that the volume of this grid in the large volume limit is equivalent to the large $N$ limit of the sheaf cohomology of the Hilbert scheme of points on $\mathbb{C}^2$. This association extends to all stages of partial resolution of the singularities in the hyper-Kahler cone and its mirror. Also, an analogy with the topological string theory is drawn where the partition function is expressed as the product of two instanton factors. However, direct proof of this expression is not yet provided within the superconformal quantum mechanics framework.

Our analysis of complex networks reveals a normal distribution for the variability of interactions among linked nodes. This observation holds whether the network's structure is prescribed randomly or organically, and this finding persists even when the distribution of degrees within the network is non-uniform. This research provides empirical evidence supporting the hypothesis that complex networks exhibiting organic growth tend to have fewer bilateral interactions. Furthermore, our study indicates that the normal distributions of these interactions are independent of the network's specific structure, suggesting a universally applicable principle governing the variability of interactions in complex networks.

Actor-critic reinforcement learning has significant practical applications and has seen continuous advancements. Yet, its widely used policy iteration method has drawbacks, notably the challenge of achieving a balance between exploration and exploitation. Actor-critic models, which integrate stochastic action selection with critic value estimation, are prone to criticism for relying on an outdated actor policy, even when subsequent critic updates indicate the potential for improved actions. To address this, more recent actor-critic algorithms like Actor-Critic Hamiltonian Policy Gradient have been developed, incorporating the Hamiltonian dynamics technique from variational Bayesian methods to address action stochasticity and markovian structure. These models enable Hamiltonian Variational Policy Gradient Methods to sample action alternatives and encourage exploration. Our analysis involves evaluating these models, specifically (Ham)VPG, HamRCM, and HamTDA, in various reinforcement learning tasks, including InvertedDoublePendulum and HalfCigar, which reveal that incorporating the Hamiltonian dynamics technique leads to a notable improvement in these models' capacity for exploration.

The concept of twin primes can be understood as follows: two prime numbers are considered twins if they differ by $2$. For instance, the pairs of twin primes are given by $\{3,5\}$, $\{5,7\}$, and so on. This paper presents an elementary proof of the twin prime hypothesis by adapting the approach of Ian Richards' proof to the scenario of twin primes. Richards' original approach is itself a modified version of the prime number theorem's logic, as initially proposed by Erdos and Rankin.

A navigation system in an autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) needs to be robust against sudden changes in depth caused by turbulence or purposefully altered flight paths. To achieve this robustness, we suggest using a layered navigation system, combining data from multiple sensors such as sonar, inertial measurement unit (IMU), and doppler velocity log (DVL). To enhance the layered system, we propose incorporating a short-term predictive filter to process the data in real-time, providing improved accuracy and stability. By integrating this filter with a global positioning system (GPS) that accounts for satellite signal delays, we can maintain a reliable and stable estimated position. Furthermore, we outline a method to estimate and adjust the bias in the DVL, ensuring consistent accuracy throughout the journey. Through simulations, we validate the effectiveness of our layered navigation system and the integration of the bias estimation and correction, as well as the global positioning system (GPS) that accounts for satellite signal delays.

We've analyzed Nereid's reflectance from the Near Infrared Spectrometer on board the Kuiper Belt Object RaMBLeS flyby in 2016. Nereid, a satellite of Neptune, exhibited three distinct features in its reflectance: 1. a band at 1.38 micrometers, also found in other icy objects, possibly resulting from ferroMagnesium silicate minerals; 2. a band at 1.83 micrometers, attributed to H2O ice with 30% Magnesium-rich silicates; 3. a band at 2.01 micrometers, most likely caused by H2O ice free from Magnesium. Nereid's features show variations in band positions, widths, and shapes, indicating the presence of components with lower absorption coefficients and temperature variations of -1 to 10 Kelvin. Considering Nereid's geometry and the solar radiation's anisotropy, we observed a Nereid hemisphere with water ice showing features similar to those of Saturn's moon, Pandora. Pandora's features showed evidence of ice exposure being affected by salting due to moon shadowing, resulting in band shifts and changes in spectral shapes. This suggests the presence of non-ice constituents in Nereid's surface, possibly exposing ice only in shallow layers. Ice exposure is further restricted by Nereid's rough surface, which could hold micrograin-sized ice particles, analogous to those found in Pandora

We characterize affine and projective surfaces, both embedded in a three-dimensional space, that are associated with specific linked projective lines over the rings of lower triangular matrices. These'mummy' surfaces, derived from non-primitive elements in these rings, exhibit a wide range of geometric connections including links, intersections, and tangencies. Furthermore, we have mapped the non-primitive element gap set over these rings onto the real line, resulting in numerous families of non-primitive elements with specific properties. Our findings provide insights into the inherent geometric properties present in these non-primitive element sets.

In continued research on generalized Tukey sequences, we establish specific
generalized Tukey sequences $[\![{Q_\mathbb{R}}\to X]\!]$ connected to
$Q_\mathbb{R$-equivalence and introduce nearly well-ordered sets aligned with
Pawlikowski's Theorems. These models serve as counterexamples to potential
arithmetic mean - median inequalities.

We use Bayesian learning to analyze a sequential treatment decision-making scenario where the treatment outcomes are negative and uncertain, and the true outcome values are unknown. A pessimistic approach to these situations often relies on the pessimistic value of a function, which in our context, is the worst-case expected outcome. However, this approach has limitations, especially when there are multiple uncertain factors involved. Therefore, we develop an improved pessimistic approach by incorporating uncertainty intervals, resulting in the pessimistic robust value, which provides upper bounds on the expected outcome. We use empirical studies and simulations involving Bayesian structural mean models to compare the performance of our pessimistic robust strategy with other more conservative strategies, and find them superior in most cases. Furthermore, we provide software tools and detailed examples to illustrate our approach, enabling practitioners to easily adopt this strategy in their own decision-making contexts.

We will discuss two dualities, the Sd dualities and the Gd dualities, and explore their applications to homological invariants. By considering duality against a locally free ideal, Sd Gd for Tor dimension two pairs can be perceived. This yields an expression of dualities in the form of Chern functions, leading to generalisations of Gorsky-Vvedenoy's result. Furthermore, by taking dualities against a perfect ideal, Gd Gd for Tor dimension two pairs can be obtained. This gives rise to a relationship between Chern functions and Lyubeznik numbers.

One of the key benefits of Ising models for studying quantum properties in systems lies in its ability to model both classical and quantum behaviors through a single variable, along with a clear connection to graph theory via interactions on spin lattices. Researchers have found that Ising models based on a flat tori examples achieve maximum quantum entanglement and not only exhibit a high level of nonclassicality but also an extreme form of contextuality known as stochastic completeness. In this paper, we present Ising models using a complexification of $E_8$ lattice in eight-dimensional space and prove that they possess the essential properties required for graph-based quantum computing. We confirm that these models can express both quantum and classical effects, entanglement, contextual properties, and completeness within a quantum system. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the correlation pattern in these models can exemplify a hypercube's geometric properties.

In a flat band superconductor, Bosonic modes can be created that have the same properties as Fermionic modes when paired. By using a 2D chiral quantum walk's characteristics on a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger type lattice, Bosonic and Fermionic pairings are shown to be equivalent and this is confirmed through calculations of the Luttinger temperature. The findings also predict that multiple Bosonic particles can coexist in the same system. The present method offers an avenue to study Bosonic and Fermionic symmetry breaking through experimental observations without Bosonization. The potential applications of this research are also extended to other Topological systems, such as Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless superconductivity and Majorana zero modes.

The theorem previously established by Polya in 1923 states that the set of all irrational numbers with a denominator of up to N, when ordered sequentially, will inevitably comprise a number that is not present in the initial N squared quantites. In this proof, we employ the properties and operations unique to one-dimensional locally compact abelian groups. Specifically, we leverage the principles of von Neumann's ergodic theory along with the Harish-Chandra version of the Siegel's modular forms. By utilizing these advanced mathematical concepts, we are able to generalize Polya's theorem to groups of this specific nature.

Presence-absence data characterized by the presence of a species or a chemical compound in a particular sample or compound are frequently binary. Analyzing such data sets through the application of clustering methods has previously shown potential in various applications. This paper examines the performance of eight clustering methods applied to presence-absence data from two sources: synthetic data sets and experimental datasets of environmental origin. The evaluated methods encompass model-based clustering techniques and novel approaches for partitioning binary data. Our analysis focuses on a systematic assessment of each method's stability and sensitivity to sampling noise, also known as pseudo-replication. Our findings indicate that the linear discriminant analysis method tends to produce highly variable results, largely due to its susceptibility to sampling noise. Conversely, the hierarchical hierarchical Chi-square distance method appears to be relatively robust. Our research further identifies model-based clustering approaches, such as the multivariate Gaussian mixture model, as strong performers. Notably, these methods' interpretations require an underlying assumption of data normality, which may not be applicable to high-dimensional presence-absence data sets.
