Our research further reveals that methods utilizing random forests or support vector machines classifiers, such as the random forest presence-absence clustering method, can produce highly variable results, largely due to the instability of these algorithms when applied to binary data sets. Overall, our analysis suggests that model-based clustering approaches, such as the multivariate Gaussian mixture model, can provide reliable results and are worthy of additional development and research.

In recent years, salient object detection using deep neural networks has received significant attention. Due to the superiority of large-scale image datasets over scarce datasets, researchers have concentrated on developing large-scale image datasets. Nevertheless, the process of creating large datasets is time-consuming and costly. In contrast, very few neural network-based approaches have been developed for salient object detection utilizing depth information, even though it has been proven to be valuable in improving salient object detection results. To efficiently utilize depth information, we propose an innovative, neural network-based approach that does not require additional parameters or complex design. By leveraging a unified framework incorporating both feature extraction and refinement modules, our approach can deliver excellent results for both RGB and RGB-D salient object detection tasks, particularly when paired with large-scale datasets. We evaluated our approach on three publicly available datasets and achieved remarkable results, surpassing 21 recent state-of-the-art methods in nearly all cases.

In this study, two different strategies were applied to the Aggressive Detection (Adversarial Aggressive Tweets) subtask.  The initial approach utilized BERT-based models, including BERT, BERT-NN, BERT-LF, BERT-NN-LF, BERT-LF-NN, and BERT-LF-NN-LF, all trained on the provided data. The second method involved combining two support vector machines, trained on different data sets, including the Wikipedia Annotation Campaign and the CrowdFlower Dataset.  Our UM-IU@LING systems ranked 74th and 75th based on Macro F1 Score.  While the BERT-based model did not enhance performance over the SVMs, this model exhibited greater efficiency and scalability.  Therefore, this system was prioritized for submission.  Notably, our BERT-LF-NN-LF model achieved a 0.0486 increase in Macro F1 Score compared to the baseline.

We present new relationships between certain classes of nonzero Hermitian and
permanental-capable (that is, nonnegative semidefinite) matrices in terms of
quantum systems. These classes include matrices with symmetric and antisymmetric
properties. Specifically, we establish that a Hermitian matrix is completely
symmetric if and only if a related quotient matrix is also completely symmetric.
Similarly, we demonstrate that a Hermitian matrix is completely antisymmetric if
and only if a related quotient matrix shares this property as well. Furthermore,
we find that a matrix is permanental-capable if and only if its quotients based on
symmetric and antisymmetric matrices have this capability too.

We propose a novel approach to reconstructing computed tomography (CT) scans while considering multiple energy spectra, noise reduction, and decomposition of materials. To achieve this, we formulate a mathematical model that combines CT data with various spectral weights and noise levels as variables. Since this problem exhibits non-convexity, we divide it into sub-problems to provide stable and computable solutions. These sub-problems involve maximizing a constraint-linear function, which we show can be solved efficiently. We validate our method by applying it to simulated and real-world data, and demonstrate its performance through quantitative evaluations. Notably, our approach allows for simultaneous material decomposition, which is not possible with existing CT reconstruction methods.

Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with minimal preparation is complicated due to language and formatting variations, but also suffers from a lack of diverse data, especially in languages that use non-standard scripts. Although synthetic data can alleviate this issue, existing approaches usually rely on pre-trained models and generate data in batches. This paper presents a novel self-learnt technique to produce high-quality synthetic training data, enabling a direct mapping from handwriting to labels without needing any prior knowledge. Additionally, since batch-based approaches can't provide single instances adaptively, this paper also proposes a unified generator that integrates both handwriting and label representations. Due to the model and dataset dependencies, this technique can't be used with existing HTR benchmarks. As such, the code and a new dataset are provided, but not included here. When applied to a real-world scenario with the Modern Greek language and Greek alphabet, the method demonstrates the efficacy of the technique by surpassing state-of-the-art results on the used evaluation benchmark.

To study heavy nuclei, researchers integrate different computational methods to alleviate the spallation problem, utilizing calculated or measured values for the 54Fe nucleus as a reference. However, utilizing measured values poses uncertainty and might introduce an equilibrium condition if the reference nucleus is in equilibrium but has different masses, affecting final results. To circumvent these issues, this work proposes using a detailed ab initio calculation of 54Fe as a foundation, leveraging the integrated framework by ab initio methods. The study, focusing on structure and binding, encompasses a wide range of nuclei from tin to lead. It's crucial to note that the integrated framework isn't a new method but rather demonstrates that ground-state properties can be accurately predicted through combined configurations, even for complex nuclei. The framework's potential to model complex nuclei opens doors for further research, and the integrated method is compared to other established methods, such as the Hartree-Fock-Yukawa model, showing significant improvement in predicting the 54Fe nucleus's binding energy.

Topological properties of quantum systems can be understood through various concepts, which are often linked to electromagnetic waves or particle scattering. A notable connection exists between these concepts and geometric structures. Topological quantum numbers can be conceptualized as charges, gaps function as potential differences, and curvatures are related to energy variations. This work explores these connections within the SSH model, revealing that linking topological concepts to geometric structures provides a unified and intuitive understanding of the system's topology.

A continuous map $\varphi: \mathbb{D} \to \mathbb{D}$ induces a compact mapping from $H^2(\mathbb{D})$ to $H^2(\mathbb{D})$ if and only if it is a biholomorphic mapping of the unit disk $\mathbb{D}$ onto itself or has a fixed point within $\mathbb{D}$. We have extended this result to higher-dimensional $n$-dimensional bounded convex domains by considering a different scenario. A continuous map $\varphi: \mathbb{D} \to \mathbb{D}$ that is biholomorphic or has a fixed point within $\mathbb{D}$ also induces a compact mapping from $H^2(\mathbb{D})$ to $H^2(\mathbb{D})$. Furthermore, we have explored the relationship between the compactness of such mappings and the analytic behavior of the disks they map, as well as the topological characteristics of their images within the unit disk $\mathbb{D}$. We have found that a disk with a biholomorphic map or a map having a fixed point has analytic properties distinct from those of a non-contractible disk with a contraction map. We have identified the necessary and sufficient topological conditions that allow the compact mapping of a disk to be composed with a holomorphic mapping of a convex domain, and thus the compact mapping of a holomorphic curve within that

In this calculation, we demonstrate that the flat superspace method accurately yields the dual supergravity field equations for the AdS$_5 \times$ S$^5$ background, when applied to a specific set of solutions. We then verify that the dual supergravity theory adheres to the principles of general relativity and supersymmetry, and that it possesses a symmetries-driven conservation of supersymmetry, which facilitates the integration of the field equations. We also derive the dual supergravity action through the flat superspace formalism and show that it agrees with the standard AdS/S$^5$ supergravity action, when expressed in the Chern-Simons form. We note that all of these results are specifically applicable to the type IIB formalism.

In order to efficiently utilize a GPU's massive number of threads during execution, developers must create objects such as arrays, matrices, and images, necessitating memory allocation. However, the existing memory allocation mechanisms on GPUs are inflexible and fail to accommodate the varied memory requirements of modern GPU applications, resulting in underutilization of the processor. The inability to dynamically allocate and manage memory on a per-element basis leads to unnecessary reallocations of larger memory blocks, causing waste and slowing down the program. The inability to allocate memory on a sub-element basis leads to users employing workarounds such as using a fixed-sized array to hold variable amounts of data, known as slacking, which causes code complexity and inefficiencies. We introduce a new dynamic memory allocator, called DynaSOAr, which is designed specifically for object-oriented programming on GPUs and is capable of allocating memory on a sub-element basis. The allocator is tailored to fit a GPU's memory hierarchy by allowing the allocation of contiguous chunks of memory at arbitrary addresses within a GPU's memory space. We show that DynaSOAr's novel allocation strategy allows it to avoid moving already allocated memory, thus outperforming existing memory allocators by as much as 10 times and facilitating the development of efficient GPU-based object-oriented programming environments.

We introduce the $U(1)_X$ models of fermion charge quantization, derived from
the $SO(10)$ framework, which incorporates three right-handed zero-mode
Wilson lines to define the $U(1}_X$ gauge symmetry. Furthermore, the
Standard Model gauge $SU(3)_c \otimes SU(2)_L \otimes U(1)_Y$ charges are
generated via two left-handed zero-modes incorporating the Clercq-Slave procedure
for the left-handed zero-modes. We analyze the possible combinations of
Wilson lines that define the $U(1)_X$ gauge symmetry, identifying one unique
model based on previously proposed $SO(10)$ embeddings of the doublet-triplet
masses. In contrast, numerous other combinations of Wilson lines are influenced by
the $(M_R, \kappa_R)$ parameters of $SO(10)$ grand unification, which may offer
additional testability to the $U(1)_X$ models.

Researchers examined the mechanical properties of a straw-like structure subjected to internal pressure, using advanced instrumental techniques such as high-resolution computed tomography (HR-CT). By applying different stress levels and monitoring the structure's response, they studied its material properties and how they vary depending on the presence of imperfections. This research is crucial for understanding and mitigating the effects of stress on small diameter pipes, particularly in biolab applications where pressure changes can cause mechanical damage and compromise safety.

Recent advances in probabilistic learning have highlighted a disconnect between model uncertainty and prediction uncertainty, prompting proposals for incorporating set-valued models within Bayesian learning frameworks. This leads to two different uncertainty measures: model uncertainty (output uncertainty) and epistemic uncertainty (sample uncertainty). The Credal Bayesian framework seeks to combine set-valued models with probabilistic learning by incorporating both uncertainties. However, this results in computationally intractable optimization problems. In this study, we introduce novel techniques to provide weak guarantees for Credal Bayesian losses, leveraging the properties of probabilistic circuits. Specifically, we show that constraint relaxation over the space of probabilistic circuits yields an efficient approximation of marginal losses, thereby enabling training of Credal Bayesian models. Furthermore, we derive strong concentration inequalities for prediction and prediction uncertainty. Our approach enables the practical training of Credal Bayesian models. Our experimental findings validate the efficacy of the proposed method.

In systems with a potential gradient and superfluids lacking a local equilibrium state, we observe oscillations in the center of mass, driven by the acceleration of the gradient. These oscillations emerge as long-lived, stationary waves localized near the center of mass, characterized by a fixed phase throughout the system. Additionally, we discuss the observation of oscillations in superfluids and propose a notable experiment involving Bose-Einstein condensates under harmonic oscillation.

In a generalised quadrangle, a code is a subset of the vertices with its minimum distance determined by the shortest path between distinct elements. The distance distribution of such a code is defined by the lengths between its elements. For a linear code within a generalised quadrangle, its Delsarte-Merenkov radius is the largest possible distance in a sphere centered at a vertex. This paper discusses linear codes in quadrangles and establishes a relationship between the Delsarte-Merenkov radius and the ratio of codewords to non-codewords in a quadrangle. Additionally, the study provides examples of linear codes achieving the maximum ratio and introduces 'neighbor-transitive' codes, a new class of linear codes in quadrangles, with a predetermined distance distribution. The study also explores partial dispersions in quadrangles and their association with linear codes, providing a framework for the classification of linear codes achieving a specific distance distribution.

A young, massive star cluster called the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) ring in the Milky Way galaxy has an irregular shape due to past dynamic interactions. Research suggests that the mass distribution within this area is not uniformly spread and can be described as flatter in certain directions. To quantify the mass distribution's anisotropy, a two-dimensional correlation function method was applied to spatial data from the CMZ. Based on this analysis, the mass anisotropy in the CMZ was determined and compared to similar areas in the galaxy. This method can be applied to other spatial data sets to determine anisotropy.

To effectively utilize X-ray absorption spectroscopy, particularly in high-fluence experiments, it is crucial to minimize electron density within the sample during excitation. An optimized rate equation model, accounting for both internal and external electron collisions, is presented to simulate non-linear X-ray absorption spectra. The model offers valuable insights for evaluating how the sample's electronic state develops over time in response to increasing X-ray flux. By utilizing this model, the threshold fluence that triggers significant ionization and autoionization processes can be identified. The model's results will be corroborated by experimental data collected using the Diamond light source.

A microtemperature sensor design has been developed using a standard 0.5$\mu$m CMOS process. This sensor efficiently converts temperature to a digital format, utilizing minimal energy and occupying a small area. The temperature range of the design can be adjusted through a binary input. We have successfully demonstrated two temperature sensors, one with a -40{\deg}C to 125{\deg}C range and another with a -55{\deg}C to 125{\deg}C range. These sensors offer exceptional performance characteristics, including a 0.44KS/b per second data rate, 0.24{\deg}C resolution, and {\pm}1.4{\deg}C accuracy, all powered by 1.6VS/supply voltage. The design's energy efficiency has been optimized, reaching a record 1.06nJ per conversion and 0.06nJ per degree performance.

Quantum entanglement, a pivotal concept in quantum science, holds immense promise for future quantum technologies. Despite extensive research, numerous quantum systems remain unsuitable for entanglement generation due to limitations in existing methods. A new approach, known as quantum scissors, enables the extraction and modification of entangled states derived from spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC), a widely available entangled resource. We integrate this technique with a technique called polarization framing to create a new device for generating polarized entangled photons. The new device can create entangled states of various polarization configurations rapidly and efficiently without the need for complex manipulation of SPDC. Additionally, it can create entangled states with specific properties, such as alignment of horizontal and vertical polarization modes, without the need for sophisticated measurement techniques. This new device has the potential to enable a range of applications in quantum information processing, including quantum computing, quantum teleportation, and quantum cryptography, by providing access to entangled photons in a reliable and predictable manner.

Researchers have intensively studied Euclidean spanners - geometric versions of networks that satisfy specific distance ratios. These geometric networks often have advantages in applications like caching, distributed computing, and geometric data repositories. In contrast to the vast number of studies on exact geometric spanners, virtual geometric spanners received relatively little attention. We developed the first virtual spanner based on pairwise shortest paths in 3D Euclidean space with a constant factor of O(log^2 k). We also found an additive 3-approximation for exact geometric spanners in 3D Euclidean space. Our methods include Minkowski sums with disks and spheres that may be useful in other applications. We studied and analyzed the computational complexity of constructing and approximating geometric spanners. Our results imply that exact geometric 3-disk spanners are either inherently difficult to construct or can be computed exactly in O(k^gamma log^3 k) time for a specific constant gamma.

Accurate classification of IoT devices is a critical requirement, with implications extending to security and data protection. Research has primarily focused on effective feature sets for identification, but the feasibility of utilizing these features on resource-constrained devices has not been thoroughly considered. We investigated the impact of feature selection on resource utilization, implementing a novel approach that combines dimensionality reduction with efficient feature extraction. Our approach incorporates information theoretic uncertainty to prioritize features with the greatest identification value while minimizing redundant information. Compared to existing methods, our approach achieves comparable or better accuracy while significantly reducing feature count, resulting in substantial memory and computational savings.

Godel modal logic's complex model theory and the associated algebraic approach are explored in this research. We introduce classes of relational structures that correspond to modal logics extending Godel modal logic, while also defining corresponding classes of modal algebras. By showing that these classes are complete for their respective modal logics, we validate our approach. Specifically, we analyze Godel modal logic and four of its extensions: Kmbl, Kr0, Kr, and Grmbl. The study demonstrates that these logics can be associated with complex relational structures, which have a rich topology, and correspondingly complex modal algebras. Unlike classical or intuitionistic logic, the relationship between these structures and their topologies is not straightforward in Godel modal logic. However, by examining the complex model theory and the associated algebraic approach, we can identify key properties that enable reliable topological constructions in the presence of negation.

This research presents a novel and efficient framework for machine translation (MT) that leverages pre-trained bilingual models and a range of external resources, such as dictionaries and knowledge graphs, to achieve high-quality word alignments quickly. By combining insights from MT and natural language processing (NLP), we develop a dictionary-based alignment model that effectively utilizes bilingual dictionaries and knowledge graphs to predict word alignments. Additionally, we introduce a novel alignment predictor, based on target-side to source-language character sequence mapping, which utilizes tens of thousands of training examples to optimize performance. We effectively integrate our approaches and showcase their effectiveness using real-world datasets, demonstrating that they outperform standard word alignment tools and are suitable for both small and large datasets.

A distorted resolvent, a variant of the resolvent of a maximally monotone operator, is used to demonstrate the existence of Nash equilibria in two distinct situations. Firstly, it is shown that any Nash equilibrium of a finite Nash game can be reconstructed using the distorted resolvent and the underlying operator's maximally monotone component. Secondly, it is proved that under certain conditions, which include compactness and convexity, the distorted resolvent enables the construction of Nash equilibria for continuous Nash games through a limit process involving the resolvent of the operator's maximally monotone part.

We employed the population symphony code (PopSyCLE) to simulate how dark energy, potentially in the form of primordial black holes, influences the universe's cosmological parameters and observable predictions. PopSyCLE uses a Markov Chain Monte Carlo method to analyze a variety of UV-sensitive observational data, including the cosmic microwave background and supernovae observations, in addition to cosmic shear and Hubble acceleration data. Our simulations with PopSyCLE considered primordial black holes as a form of dark energy, assuming a physically constrained model with three free parameters: the dark energy density, a parameter describing PBH mass function skewness, and the PBH mass. Our results indicate that including PBHs in dark energy enhances the fit to supernovae and Hubble acceleration data, while compromising the cosmic microwave background fit; however, these improvements are mainly evident when allowing the PBH mass function to be skewed, as this enables a better accommodation of data inconsistencies. Our best-fit models using cosmic microwave background, supernovae, and Hubble acceleration data suggest a PBH mass of approximately $10^{-17}$ or $10^{-18}$ ounces, in the case of a symmetric or skewed distribution, respectively. These studies demonstrate how PopSyCLE can effectively model PBH dark energy and accommodate various observational data sets.

In a system where spherical bodies of uniform size in three-dimensional space arrange themselves in the most energetically stable configurations, we find that some of these arrangements exhibit splay modulations while remaining in these energetically stable states. However, when subjected to external rotations, these systems transition through various phases, some featuring standing waves and others involving globally synchronized rotations. Interestingly, for certain specific conditions, we observe the emergence of left-right asymmetric rotation patterns. Furthermore, our analysis has revealed the presence of scaling parameters, enabling us to study how the characteristics of these rotating phases change when the number of spherical bodies is modified. Additionally, we provide a theoretical framework, coupled with numerical simulations, to investigate dynamically unstable configurations and their rhythmic movements in these complex many-body systems.

Decompositions of spherical surface data or signals into simplifiable components have numerous applications in data analysis. The techniques employed in such decompositions often resemble Kalman filter-like algorithms, which break down complex processes or measurements into more manageable parts. This study develops a straightforward method for decomposing static field data, such as satellite imagery, into meaningful components. The proposed method is inspired by Kalman filter recursion but is optimized for faster computation, making it suitable for large-scale real-world applications. The resulting decomposition is then used to improve the accuracy of spherical surface data interpolation and signal reconstruction.

Our concept of visualizing quantum states relies on the ability of undetected photon pairs to form images, circumventing the need for entanglement. By leveraging single-pixel quantization, we can smoothly represent both amplitude and phase of an image, ultimately resulting in undetected photon pairs that reconstruct the original quantum object. Our method consistently outperforms prior approaches, yielding substantial improvements in fidelity with fewer undetected photons.

The interaction between a liquid foam and a solid surface involves complex processes influenced by the friction between the two materials in question. This study investigates how the frictional interaction between a liquid foam and a solid surface is affected by the presence of surfactants. When surfactants are applied to a silicone oil and water mixture forming the foam, we observe a substantial decrease in the frictional force required to move a solid through the foam. This effect is more pronounced when the surfactants reduce the surface tension of the foam further, indicating that the decreased friction is primarily caused by a reduction in the foam's viscosity. When the surfactants are insufficient, leading to an increased range of values for the surface tension, the frictional force exhibits an intricate relationship with this variation. A possible explanation for this complex behavior is that the frictional force is influenced by two competing processes: the friction induced by the blocking of flow channels at higher surface tensions and an increased ease of flow due to reduced bubble sizes at lower surface tensions.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer classification and lesion counting. A hybrid approach combining deep learning and feature selection methods was utilized to identify the most informative features for classification among multiple potential features derived from images and metadata. To address class imbalance, a focal loss function was implemented. For task 2, focusing on identifying atypical lesions, the deep learning model was modified to include an additional output layer and corresponding loss function to optimize multi-task performance. To handle outlier samples, the 1-nearest neighbor classifier was adjusted to calculate the 1-nearest neighbor distance with leverage consideration of data density around each class boundary.

We measured the lifetime of electrons that have been perturbed in sodium, a metal with very weak electronic interactions. Our findings agree with theoretical predictions from the relaxation-time approximation that uses the density of states near the Fermi level. Additionally, we calculated the density of states and found that it exhibits fluctuations at very short ranges due to sodium's complex structure. These fluctuations are a result of the large density of magnetic impurities in pure sodium, which can be minimized by adding small amounts of gadolinium to it.

One dimensionally confined systems such as ideal gas, harmonic oscillator and van der Waals spheres exhibit diverse expansion behaviors following release from confinement. Our approach combines the fundamental principles of Lagrangian to develop a straightforward analytical formula for calculating the phase space volume variation, applicable to a broad class of confined systems. For systems without potential energy, this technique reduces to a simple method that relies on the Hamiltonian's conservative property. When coupled with the concept of Hamiltonian paths, this approach enables the calculation of final phase space distribution for systems like ideal gas undergoing free expansion, even in situations where the Lagrangian cannot be determined.

Kontsevich's structure theorem describes the local expansion of a formal power series that defines a bilinear map, and it shows that these weights can be represented by graphs based on a local coordinate system's coordinates and their derivatives. When we consider a specific structure theorem application to a symplectic 2-form, we can analyze the weights by examining the local linear independence of its elements, which can be described through the connection matrix's curvature. By applying graph theoretical methods to the curvature's eigenvalues and invariant factors, we can calculate the curvature's local dimension and derive a combinatorial formula for the structure theorem's weights. This approach can also be extended to consider non-integer values of the curvature's local dimension.

We explore the dynamics of a weakly nonlinear woodpile and diatomic granular chain to establish conditions for exponential growth, specifically scenarios where localized disturbances amplify. By transforming the system into a mathematical equation, we leverage the properties of Nanoptera from number theory to derive necessary conditions for exponential growth. While primary instability is inherent in both systems, we reveal that secondary instability emerges in the woodpile configuration but not in its diatomic counterpart, ultimately determining that exponential growth occurs in both configurations but at different rates.

Our research expands upon cosmological collider physics, an approach that employs perturbation equations to analyze nonlinear density disparities in the early universe. By leveraging the equations, we're able to identify distinct patterns or features resulting from various primordial sources, which can be compared to the characteristics of observed features. This methodology enables us to infer details about a potential feature's initial formation, despite limited information about its subsequent development, by utilizing the features themselves. Specifically, we've established two essential properties, termed primal mass and primal mass-dimensional count, which respectively denote the initial mass density and the number of independent variables associated with a feature. A feature's primal mass indicates its density level during the early universe, while its primal mass-dimensional count signifies the number of parameters describing that density, ultimately influencing the feature's distinguishable patterns. By establishing these properties, we're able to analyze a variety of features and classify them, laying the groundwork for inferring a feature's properties based on its characteristics in future work.

The Accordion graph is introduced and examined with a focus on its properties. This graph structure has symmetric properties and can be represented by a quartic circulant graph, specifically $C_{16}(\[1, 5, 11, 13\])$. This alignment suggests that the Accordion graph is a pairing of the Hamiltonian cycles within this circulant graph, and this observation provides a method for identifying the Hamiltonian cycles of the Accordion graph. Additionally, it has been verified that the Accordion graph is distinct from the Cartesian product of two cycles, $C_{9} \times C_{11}$. This distinction establishes the Accordion graph as a unique graph structure with this particular product graph as its only non-isomorphic counterpart.

In quantum walks with three possible states, researchers have studied the dynamics of probability distributions and wave functions using scaling principles derived from renormalization group techniques. This study extends that work by examining the global behavior of these distributions and wave functions in three-state quantum walks. Our analysis shows that at any given time, the support of the wave function's domain grows proportionally to $t^{\alpha_q}$, where $\alpha_q=4$ and $t$ is the time. Conversely, the probability distribution's support grows proportionally to $t^{\alpha_p}$, where $\alpha_p=3$. Additionally, our results indicate that both the wave functions and probability distributions display symmetrical scaling properties in relation to the initial conditions used.

This paper introduces PVNet, a Self-Guided Vision Transformer (SVT) network that is enhanced by a property predictor head. By encoding multiple property maps into the network, PVNet enhances existing SVT models by providing additional contextual information to the model. To achieve this, PVNet incorporates a simple, efficient design that includes just three extra trainable parameters. The effectiveness of PVNet is demonstrated across three challenging scenarios: (1) generating multiple outputs from a single input; (2) generating multiple outputs from multiple inputs; and (3) multiple output productions often conflicting with each other. Experiments conducted on various benchmark datasets consistently demonstrate the superior performance of PVNet over existing SVT models, showcasing its versatility and robustness in diverse down-stream tasks.

A cosmological model is developed using a novel equation of state for a complex dark fluid comprised of non-relativistic matter and radiation, whose interaction is mediated by spatially uniform friction. This dark fluid's total energy density remains constant over time, whereas the matter component generates energy due to friction, thereby offsetting the radiation component's energy. Assuming the dark energy density is constant, we demonstrate that this model produces a universe with no big bang singularity, followed by a period of acceleration. We also analyzed phase portraits to determine existence and stability. Our findings reveal that this model produces a universe with no singularity, accompanied by acceleration, consistent with observed data.

We present a straightforward proof that in three or more dimensions, the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations has an issue when using Sobolev spaces and certain types of Lorentz spaces, specifically those represented by the notation $L_{p,x}^{s,1}$ or $\Lambda^{s}_{p,x}$ with $p\in [1,2]$ and $s>1+\frac{1}{p}$ being a real number. This proof is simpler and based on earlier work by Catale and Muration, in contrast to previous arguments found in the literature.

Emergent semantics in large language models stem from extensive training, yet current techniques for transferring semantics to novel tasks often rely on additional fine-tuning stages or input/output manipulations. We propose the steady creator, a generator-pretrainer paradigm, to effectively seed semantics and enable efficient task adaptation. By capturing high-level semantic structures in representations through self-supervised pretraining and maintaining them intact during downstream task training, the steady creator achieves significant performance enhancements over existing methods. Notably, it yields a substantial boost of over 100% improvement in certain cases. Additionally, the steady creator's increased robustness and reduced fine-tuning requirements align with the principles of efficient algorithms, making it a desirable approach for adapting large language models to diverse tasks and domains.

Recent advancements in image processing technology have enabled the development of reversible image concealment techniques, allowing both concealed images and original contents to be accurately recovered after implementation. Unfortunately, traditional concealment methods often necessitate permanent modification to the input data, resulting in irreversible changes. In contrast, reversible concealment methods, characterized by recovery rates exceeding 98%, have become increasingly common. A novel approach is presented in this study that incorporates Bayesian neural networks to dynamically determine the optimal convolution kernel for an adaptive and efficient concealment method. Experimental results confirm the superior reversible performance of this method in comparison to state-of-the-art techniques.

Our research investigates the significance of the $J/\psi$ decays into invisible particles and gamma plus invisible particles in the framework of effective field theories. By utilizing experimental data from the LHCb and BESIII experiments, we established constraints on low-energetic operators related to neutrino production and dark energy. Our study reveals that these operators result in a phase shift between $J/\psi$ and its antiparticle, making it potentially detectable in advanced experiments such as the PANDA project. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the operator structure of neutrino production has the capacity to be determined, whereas it is impossible for dark energy, even in the presence of hypothetical inviscous dark energy with non-zero Compton wavelength. Moreover, our study establishes that the virtual loop particles in the operator connecting a gamma radiation and two W bosons has mass greater than $M_W$.

Recent studies using the Coronal Angular Distribution (CAD) technique have revealed extensive bright structures on the sun's corona, however their underlying physical mechanisms remain unclear. Our research aims to establish whether these bright spots have a magnetic origin by demonstrating that their distribution patterns are indeed two-parted, consistent with the characteristics of correlated and independently varying magnetic field components often present in complex magnetic fields. By applying a Gaussian mixture model to analysis of CAD data, we were able to separate and identify the separate distributions of emission intensity and temperature, providing strong evidence that these bright structures are rooted in solar magnetism.

Human vision can integrate information across time and space to identify moving objects, a process known as dynamic object identification. Some computer models, like deep neural networks, excel in this area, but it's unclear if they accurately replicate the human visual system. This study investigates whether minimal clips, the simplest visual presentations of moving objects, can provide insights crucial for developing effective dynamic object identification models. By examining two widely used models, a simple and a complex deep neural network, we explored their performance on minimal clips, focusing on whether they can learn to recognize objects based on coherent motion cues, like those used by humans. Our results reveal that both models struggle with object identification in complex scenarios, unlike humans, who excel in these situations. Our research important because object tracking and identification have significant practical value and can inform future model development with insights from human visual processing.

Dark matter, comprising approximately 85% of total mass-energy density in the universe, remains undiscovered and is not accounted for by the Standard Model. A novel theory proposes that dark matter is comprised of magnetic monopoles, which are stabilized by local symmetry and weighted differently in magnetic fields, resulting in masses that vary with scale. This scale-dependent density, combined with local anisotropy, allows for the possibility of dark matter's presence in small quantities at smaller scales while allowing larger structures to form. As a result, dark matter's distribution is not uniform across all scales. In the context of galaxy clusters, this theory may provide a mechanism to explain their persistent magnetic fields. Additionally, the theory of milli-magnetic monopole dark matter offers a potential explanation for the observed anomalies in cosmic microwave background radiation, featuring large-scale anisotropy and featuring temperature differences between even and odd parity modes.

Predicting climate variables over extensive areas and long periods of time demands sophisticated models that can effectively capture both spatial and temporal correlations. Despite state-of-the-art models like transformers exceling in these areas, they are often prohibitively computationally expensive and impractical for practical applications. A new model has been proposed which combines the advantages of transformer architecture with efficient neural network designs, featuring localized attention mechanisms and hierarchical prediction features. It specifically utilizes shifted window attention to prioritize context relevance and uses a scaled attention to prioritize high-magnitude variables. When tested on climate datasets, it outperformed existing models in accuracy and achieved a notable reduction in computational requirements.

Three-Higgs-doublet models that incorporate an $S_3$ symmetry group have several advantages, including the avoidance of "flavor changing neutral currents" that are not in line with current experimental data. Furthermore, these models have the capability to provide an explanation for the recently discovered neutrino oscillation data and observed anomalies. Notably, they are able to have dark matter that is stable, a feature that is lacking in the majority of the "three doublet models". In this study, we thoroughly examine the possibility of having dark matter in models with $S_3$ symmetry, and during our investigation, we come across not one, but two options. In the first option, we have dark matter that is a fractionally charged component, whereas in the second, we have a naturally stable dark matter candidate that arises due to an imposed "accidental" $Z_2$ symmetry, and has properties similar to neutrinos. We also present the results of two sets of numerical calculations that demonstrate the suitability of the model parameters to their respective datasets.

The PPT quadrilateral hypothesis emerges as a simplified version of the local optimality principle for quantum computation after excluding the possibility of quantum advantage via low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes and quantum repetition codes. By examining conformal quantum field theory and using numerical methods such as the quantum approximate optimization algorithm, research finds that the PPT quadrilateral hypothesis likely holds. In fact, the underlying assumption that PPT states form a convex cone also appears to be valid. If proven, the PPT quadrilateral hypothesis would serve as strong evidence for the local optimality of quantum computation, thereby excluding the possibility of quantum advantage via no-deletion or low-density parity-check codes.

In neurons, the transportation system relies on molecular substances being continuously supplied and removed to ensure a wide range of signals can be transmitted. To maintain the transportation process, the neuron regulates the amount of available substances by adjusting the settings of the transportation equipment. We develop a mathematical model that utilizes optimization techniques to represent the transportation process and equipment adjustments, with a unique solution representing a normal, functioning transportation system. By constraints, we simulate the filtering of substances at the base of the neuron and investigate how these constraints impact the transportation system's functionality. Our study focuses on developing efficient solution methods for the optimized equipment settings and exploring the effects of filtering constraints. We utilize numerical simulations to investigate the interplay between the transportation system's parameters and the consequences of congestion caused by filtering overload, analyzing the implications of such congestion on the transportation process and equipment maintenance.

Our research identifies network motifs, specific recurring patterns in the connections between companies within an industry, as key indicators of successful finance-related predictions. By analyzing these motifs, we demonstrate their ability to forecast the direction of stock price movements and other financially related outcomes. To construct these patterns, we utilize the Maximal Random Subgraph approach, a state-of-the-art algorithm. Our findings are presented in three phases, each of which uses a variation of this method to discover patterns in different contexts: initially, patterns are discovered directly; in a second phase, patterns are discovered after reducing the complexity of the network through dimensionality reduction; in a third phase, patterns associated with successful predictions are first identified, and then used to construct new patterns by combining those that, alone, do not foretell financially related outcomes. A comprehensive evaluation in three different datasets illustrates the effectiveness of our approach, where results show that patterns discovered can accurately forecast financially related outcomes in anticipation pricing tasks, outperforming a top-performing model's performance. Our work contributes novel patterns for financially related outcomes, and showcases the feasibility of network motifs as indicators of prediction targets. Our study also highlights potential avenues of research, such as leveraging domain-specific features to further improve pattern discovery.

The merger of a 1.38 solar mass white dwarf with a 7.25 solar mass black hole was simulated using the ASTROBEAR code in this study. We found that the white dwarf's matter was able to penetrate the black hole's event horizon because its mass was sufficient to overcome the black point's gravitational pull. This resulted in the white dwarf's destruction through a process known as accretion disruption, which causes emissions. Our findings indicate that the accretion rate in this event is likely to be steady, producing steady emissions, although we did not account for emissions in this simulation. We did analyze the emissions spectrum resulting from the accretion of the white dwarf's matter into the black hole and found that the spectral emissions could reach levels as high as 10^52 erg s^-1. It's possible that these emissions could be observable using future gravitational wave missions, such as the LISA, provided the progenitor white dwarf's mass is sufficiently large. If the white dwarf's matter penetrates the black point's horizon, it could lead to the production of heavy elements, potentially large in number, through nuclear reactions, which could also be detectable. Additionally, we found that the gravitational wave signal produced in this event could be strong enough to be detectable at distances of up to 10 gigaparsecs using future gravitational wave missions, with a signal frequency ranging from millihertz to 300 kilohertz.

We analyze the formation of baryon-like di-quinquark states, denoted as $B$, in terms of irreducible representation tables of the $SU(3)$ group, and then calculate the relevant form factors for the three-body semileptonic decays of the tau particle. By applying the model of di-quinquark baryon currents, we evaluate numerical values for baryon production probabilities and examine their variation across different decay modes. Furthermore, we derive baryon formation probabilities for endogenous and exogenous di-quinquark baryon states, and also compute the corresponding spectral distribution and total decay width for the semileptonic decay of the tau particle into these baryon states along with a lepton and a photon. We compare our results with recent experimental findings and other theoretical models.

Previous studies have established the Jaccard distance as a limit case of the Kullback-Leibler distance, yet research found a different explanation for this relationship. We re-examine the model proposed in that research and modify it to obtain a broader family of parametrized functions. We first derive a revised model and then use it to explain the origin of the Tversky metric. Our study also highlights that varying the model's parameters can either increase or reverse the asymmetry and contamination present in the Tversky metric. Furthermore, we obtain a new expression for the normalized information distance and investigate its properties. We provide empirical evidence for our findings using data from social networks.

Modern deblurring methods are ineffective against real-world handwritten text within heavily blurred images. To address this, we present a novel approach combining image deblurring with handwritten text restoration using a specialized generator and classification system designed to differentiate between genuine and artificially created blurred signals. The proposed system, which includes a differential transformer, outperforms existing methods in restoring both human-generated and machine-generated movements, as evidenced by our experimental results on widely-used datasets. Additionally, we release the source code and model weights to the public, facilitating future advancements in this field.

Current molecular-based neuromorphic platforms lack the sophistication of their CMOS-based counterparts, restricting them primarily to spike-based communication. Although this limitation, if overcome, could enable low-power neural network architectures reminiscent of biological neurons. We've developed a versatile neural network model that resembles biological neurons, learning through a simple, biological-plausible algorithm. We've also implemented this model on spiking neural network architectures utilizing both analog and digital hardware, exemplified by the analog VLSI chip, Neuropixel, and digital hardware with FPGAs. Moreover, our model's effects on performance and energy consumption have been experimentally measured. Compared to conventional digital neural networks, our analog implementation exhibits a 1000x decrease in bit-rate, while still maintaining comparable error rates, and a 10x decrease in bit-rate with comparable error rates, when compared to digital neural networks.

In this research, we demonstrate the completeness of the ultrapower of arranged sets with respect to intervals, establishing a rigorous foundation for establishing completeness in the ultrapower with respect to other relations. Our findings also address a prior unsolved problem, stating that the ultrapower of arranged sets is not comparable with respect to all possible relations. Furthermore, our results are illustrated by examples of specific sequences of interval subsets.

The growing number of scientific datasets is expected to reach 100 sextillion points by 2025, making them increasingly unfeasible to work with using today's most powerful computers. This trend is exacerbated by the fact that many datasets are typically only accessed and analyzed once, often being discarded afterwards, making Reproducibility a vital concern in this field. Since computers are becoming significantly faster, the main bottleneck in data analysis is shifting towards memory bandwidth, data movement, and computation cost. This research targets these issues by developing a new approach called Dataset Profiling, which provides tailored performance suggestions specifically tailored to each scientific dataset. Our innovative technique combines three unique strategies, including: (1) finding the optimal data transformation, (2) customizing memory allocation, and (3) adapting algorithms to accommodate a dataset's distinct features, all of which are determined through our proposed profiling process, thereby enhancing Reproducibility and providing a notable performance boost in scientific simulations. Our cutting-edge framework, called Profiler, is versatile and can be applied to various programming languages, including Fortran, Python, and C, as demonstrated by our extensive experiments, which showcase an average speedup of 2.3 times across numerous benchmark datasets, ultimately enabling Reproducibility and significant performance improvements in scientific data analysis.

Hadwiger's Coloring Conjecture asserts that every graph with t colors incorporating the complete graph of t order can be tinted with t colors. In response, Finsterer proposed an alternative, less complex version: if a graph with t colors includes the complete graph of t - 1 order, it can be tinted with t colors. This revised version has been verified for graphs on at most five vertices, but not fully complex cases, although certain constraints have been imposed. Recently, Bartosz Abramowski and Krzysztof Klos kon have independently proved that if a graph with t colors includes the complete graph of t - 1 order, but with an additional restriction that the graph with t - 1 colors including the complete graph of t - 2 order can be tinted with t - 1 colors. Our research extends this result by stating that if a graph with t colors including the complete graph of t - 1 order can be tinted with t colors when the graph with t - 1 colors including the complete graph of t - 2 order can be tinted with t - 1 colors. This result has been verified for networks with at most five colors.

This research introduces a robust adaptive generalized correntropy-based algorithm for graph signal restoration, incorporating a kernel width optimization step derived from the quantization error of its binary representation. The proposed method efficiently computes the gradient of the normalized kernel's squared derivative, resulting in significantly lower computational complexity than existing adaptive correntropy-based algorithms. Furthermore, theoretical analysis confirms that the optimal kernel width corresponds to the binary representation of $2^{N-1}$, where N is the number of nodes on the graph. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed algorithm in restoring noisy graph signals, achieving superior performance with reduced computational efficiency and a wider application range than existing adaptive algorithms.

One major constraint limiting the precision of quantum signal measurements comes from the inherent limitations of classical detection methods. We have devised a novel protocol utilizing an entangled spinor interferometer that enables the creation of customized quantum states to circumvent these detection constraints. By creating customized quantum states, we can optimize measurements to be compatible with available detection methods, thereby enhancing the overall metrological outcome. Specifically, we demonstrate the ability to tailor states for both absorption and phase-sensitive detection, utilizing an entangled spinor interferometer that produces entangled light. Through customized quantum state preparation, we can optimize the standard quantum limit and consistently achieve high signal-to-noise ratios, even when utilizing low-intensity light.

We have derived a precise estimate for the first eigenvalue of the Robin Laplacian on a domain with smooth boundary in n-dimensional space. This estimate takes into account a general non-decreasing non-constant function in the Laplacian and a boundary condition that varies with the function. Our method involves studying the perturbed operator and using a variational approach, which allows us to narrow down the possible values of the eigenvalue and estimate it accurately. This research generalizes and expands previous studies on estimates for the Laplacian and Schrödinger operator.

Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) have become influential deep learning models for handling graph-based tasks. The convolutional nature in GCNNs diverges significantly from traditional CNNs, using aggregate operations like max-pooling or graph convolution, unlike the gradient-based signal propagation seen in conventional CNNs. The graph convolution operation can obscure the flow of gradients, limiting understanding. We propose a matched filtering approach to illuminate the operation, using historical kernel values to filter and propagate forward, and adapting max-pooling to reveal how features are aggregated and reduced. By visualizing the activation maps, we dissect the learning process and demonstrate how features are combined and diminished. Furthermore, we illustrate how the choice of aggregation method affects activation maps, demonstrating the complexity of features being combined. We use the visualizations to show how the learning process evolves over time and how the combination of features changes through iterative training. We achieve comparable results to current state-of-the-art methods in graph-based semantic segmentation, using Deep Graph Convolutional Network and Graph Convolutional Network with max-pooling.

In the realm of Natural Language Processing (NLP), significant advancements have been achieved with models like BERT, yet these improvements have not been translated to Dependency Parsing (DP) with contextualized representations. Our research presents a novel, deep contextualized dependency parsing approach that autonomously fine-tunes itself and adapts to data shortages. The proposed model generates synthetic tree structures and corresponding dependencies to supplement limited training data, and then employs self-learned dependencies to guide the DP tree construction. The synthetic data is generated through a stochastic process, where parent-offspring relationships are created sequentially one sentence at a time. The model also includes a self-attention mechanism allowing each token to be informed by all other tokens, thus leveraging the full contextualization of BERT. Our model can operate without manual label supervision and provides exceptional performance even with just 1,000 annotated examples, achieving results on par with state-of-the-art models trained on the full WSJ dataset. Moreover, our model shows considerable speed savings, completing a single iteration in under 2 seconds, and exhibits improved robustness and consistency compared to models trained on partially annotated data.

The light-front quark model representation, incorporating interaction effects within the bound state, is applied to describe the transition form factors for the process $B\to D\ell\nu_\ell$. Our calculation of the form factor $|F(0)|^2$ reveals agreement with phenomenological results based on CLN, AUB, and BGL analyses. Additionally, our work examines the ratio $|F(2)|^2/|F(1)|^2$ and contrasts it with existing estimates from QCD lattice regulations. The success of our approach in achieving good agreement with experimental data for various form factors suggests the potential of the light-front quark model, with interaction effects considered, as a precise tool for form factor calculations and possibly rare decay studies.

This research explores a non-reversible version of 2d Yang-Mills symmetry within the context of string theory, specifically within the framework of topological membranes. It is discovered that systems comprising topological membranes coupled to non-reversible symmetries exhibit an expansion of charges, resulting in the gratification of modular invariant conditions that originally held only at vanishing temperature. Furthermore, it is found that the non-reversible symmetry facilitates the transformation of topological membranes into Witten's string fluid, thereby enabling the incorporation of Witten's string fluid into the system. Conversely, it is observed that the non-reversible symmetry can be viewed as an extension of Witten's string fluid with temperature as a variable. Moreover, it is noted but left unproven that the non-reversible symmetry is compatible with the $\mathbb{Z}_4$ clock symmetry. Lastly, it is proposed that the non-reversible symmetry may find applications in describing systems comprising D-branes and non-reversible strings.

Researchers were initially unable to resolve whether there's a machine that can solve all problems in NP in polynomial time, regardless of the amount of memory it uses. A significant breakthrough occurred when they discovered an equivalent class of problems that can be solved by a particular type of machine that uses memory efficiently. This led them to create a new class, called LogNP, and an equivalent class, called LogCaiNP, based on a modified machine design. In this study, the teams made progress by proving two key points: First, the class LogCaiNP is equivalent to solving NP problems with restricted polynomial time on a specific type of machine; second, LogCaiNP is equal to a previously classified problem set called PCP(log, 1). These findings resolved an open question about whether LogCaiNP is restricted to a certain class of problems that can be solved with limited machine help. This new knowledge also led them to reclass a previously known problem set, called NPMV, and resulted in an equivalent classification for problem sets that can be solved by a machine that uses memory efficiently. This new knowledge also led them to reclass a previously known problem set, called NPMV, and resulted in an equivalent classification for problem sets that can be solved by a machine that uses memory efficiently.

In a compound known as pyrochlore iridates, the presence of 5d transition metals in a unique geometric arrangement suggests strong correlations and unusual electronic properties. Research on the binary iridate series, with variations of $Bi_2$ replacing $Eu_2$ in $Eu_2Ir_2O_7$, has shown that bi-bilayer $Bi_2Ir_2O_7$ displays significant time-reversal symmetry breaking through structural distortions. We observed an unexpected shift from an insulating to a metallic state as $x$ increases from 0 to 0.5 in the series $Eu_1-xBi_xIr_2O_7$ using HAXPES, indicating that this shift is not due to an increase in disorder. Our findings indicate the onset of possible unconventional superconductivity or other unusual orders in the $Bi_2Ir_2O_7$ series, and our results are complemented by first-principles calculations, which show that the insulating state in $EuIr_2O_7$ is stabilized by strong electronic correlations, while $Bi_2Ir_2O_7$ shows a significant reduction in correlation effects and an increase in band-like behavior.

We establish a two-dimensional set-valued mapping framework and establish standards for existence of various types of selections, including Lipschitz selections. This category encompasses the most relevant and important selections in the context of low dimensional set-valued mappings. The key concepts explored herein are Q-lsc set-valued mappings, specifically those with closed or bounded values, which include $\mathcal{A}$-compact, provably bounded, or locally provably bounded mappings. Our analysis of these mappings reveals they are all equivalent to having compact selections, which in turn is equivalent to having Lipschitz selections under low dimensional contexts. We examine the properties of each type of Q-lsc mapping, establish key equivalence theorems, and demonstrate that they can be characterized through local properties, thereby facilitating an analytical approach to establishing the existence of Lipschitz selections. Ultimately, our work provides an exhaustive decomposition of low dimensional set-valued mappings into a hierarchy of existence standards, effectively rendering the concept of selection redundant in this context, while also highlighting the importance of efficient procedures for achieving selections. The research also identifies a lower bound on dimensional constraints required for the existence of Lipschitz selections, which is currently set at two dimensions.

This research investigates the probability of occurrences sequences of heads and tails deriving from fair coins flips, specifically those characterized by circular and non-transitive properties in the context of (k,m,n) configurations, where the latter implies the existence of at least two different permutation orders resulting in the same sequence. By developing a combinatorial approach, expressed via the circular Kostka number, a formula is derived for the probability of observing both circular and non-transitive properties in (k,m,n) configurations with the former signified by the latter's absence. Furthermore, an associated criterion is formulated to differentiate between circular and non-transitive properties, particularly evident in situations where m equals n. In addition, this study examines the distinct cases where m equals n and equals 2, uncovering a symmetry in the associated probabilities when n is an even number and analyzing the associated row in a binary triangle matrix. Moreover, a novel distinction is made between circular and non-transitive properties in the specific context of (k,2,2) configurations, along with comprehensive numerical results obtained by exhaustive calculations for all (k,m,n) triples up to a certain limit, along with associated data on the length of the resulting binary sequences.

In the context of software composition, compile-time techniques can significantly reduce run-time complexity by eliminating unnecessary reflections. This study specifically investigates whether compile-time tools can streamline the process of setting up software frameworks, which typically involve complex interactions. To gauge the potential, we conducted an in-depth analysis of the framework setup process in four popular Java libraries: Hibernate, Spring, Apache Cassandra, and JPA. We employed strategic design patterns to integrate these frameworks, then applied compile-time transformation to optimize the setup process, ultimately comparing the results with traditional annotated approaches. The outcomes of our evaluation demonstrate that compile-time tools can indeed streamline framework setup, yielding substantial improvements in run-time performance and setup complexity. Notably, we observed a average reduction of 1.51 milliseconds in run-time complexity and an average decrease of 6.14 annotated methods required for setup, along with enhanced security and reduced risks associated with complex run-time setup processes facilitated by tools like JSP and OSGI.

Light dark matter particles, specifically those weighing less than a GeV, can be effectively detected by observing the effects of their interactions within nuclei. When light dark matter interacts with nuclei, it can cause the nucleus to react violently, releasing excessive energy as gamma rays or particle winds, indicating the nucleus has undergone a massive reaction. Alternatively, light dark matter can interact with quarks within the nucleus, resulting in an inelastic reaction that releases energy as the quark system adjusts. Such interactions can also be identified through the creation of electron-positron pairs as the quark releases energy or through the creation of scanned electrons as the quark's arrangement is altered. Consequently, dark matter interactions can manifest as excessive electron production following nuclear interactions, and such a signature offers an effective direct method for detecting sub-GeV dark matter.

In the past three decades, the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model and its associated quantum phenomena have been relatively underappreciated compared to the conventional Jaynes-Cummings model. However, the former model still holds significant interest due to its ability to describe coherent phenomena in its classical limit, in addition to featuring renowned quantum phenomena such as entanglement, transmission, and Rabi oscillations. This model's unique phase space behavior, characterized by periodic trajectories, distinguishes it from the Jaynes-Cummings model with its chaotic characteristics. Leveraging the stationary states of the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model, we successfully synchronize the phase space trajectories of both models, thereby generating periodic trajectories in the latter. Furthermore, we demonstrate the existence of Rabi oscillations and entanglement in both models, revealing that the absence of Rabi oscillations in the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model actually stems from canceling Rabi frequencies, while the amount of entanglement remains influenced by the detuning. Lastly, we investigate transmission properties in both models and their correlations.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can be complicated when the signals are distorted by noise, which often occurs in real-world recordings. Researchers have developed various techniques to remove noise from ECG signals, but many existing methods have limitations that make them difficult to use in practice. In an effort to create a more effective technique, a study developed a model based on a unique architecture of residual networks to remove noise from ECG signals. However, in an effort to improve the model's efficiency, the study modified the architecture to a Tiramisu model. The study found that the modified model significantly outperformed existing techniques in assessing inter-beat intervals, and it has the added benefit of being easily implementable in practical applications.

We've developed a theoretical model for interacting particles that move according to Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes, influenced by periodic, spatially-varying forces and stochastic forces that depend on collective behavior. In this model, each particle is represented as a finite, rotating shape with a specified size, and its movement is determined by an angular position within a force field that varies periodically. As a result, the particle's location over time can be described as a nonlinear process. Our goal is to understand how interactions between particles affect their movement patterns by analyzing the differences in movement patterns for individual particles versus those in large groups of particles. Our approach involves analyzing the fundamental characteristics of the particle's movement and deriving equations that describe how these characteristics change in response to variations in the particle count. We've established that the movement patterns for individual particles and in large groups of particles are governed by different equations, particularly when considering how quickly these patterns change. For large groups of particles, the movement patterns are highly consistent and only change slowly in response to changes in the system's underlying components. Our findings have important implications for understanding collective movement patterns in large groups of particles, and these patterns could have far-reaching implications in science and medicine when understanding phenomena like active matter.

HUMBI, a vast, freely accessible database containing diverse multiview video recordings of human body movements, has been developed. Unlike existing datasets, HUMBI distinctive approach captures the entire human body from multiple viewpoints, employing a range of cameras. This results in a distinct distribution of yaw and movement ranges in comparison to existing datasets. HUMMI, a key feature of HUMBI, is a benchmark challenge that incorporates activities like categorizing the views of new videos, estimating 3D human joint locations, and generating human body animations. This benchmark, used to evaluate existing datasets, reveals significant discrepancies in the representation of human body movements. Several important applications, such as human recreation and animation, also rely on this representation. Our research indicates that current techniques struggle with tasks related to HUMBI, opening up opportunities for more advanced models and a broader range of applications. The HUMBI dataset, view classification task, 3D human joint estimation code, and animated human body videos are all accessible online.

Deep neural language models have achieved significant success across various tasks in different genres of texts, typically developed using abundant resources. However, scripts of high-quality data are often scarce and expensive to obtain for lesser-studied languages. A novel approach has been introduced to facilitate model-independent cross-lingual transfer learning using task representations as weak supervision, which can be applied without intricate knowledge of the target language. This method relies on mapping task representations to universal indices that can be learned from distant datasets. Since these task representations are learned objectively, they remain consistent across different models, enabling effective knowledge sharing across languages. Our method was validated through successful applications in multiple English tasks, including sentiment analysis and question-answering, and can be efficiently applied to any language without tuning. When applied to Spanish models, this method yielded a 40% improvement in performance over baseline models trained solely on local data, and achieved results comparable to those of highly-trained models developed with abundant target-language data.

A robust video super-resolution method called BasicVSR has gained significant recognition for its exceptional performance and efficiency. However, the original approach had a major drawback in terms of computational complexity, which hindered its adoption in various real-world applications. The issue lies in the intricate 3D conditional propagation and feature alignment processes that are time-consuming and occupy a substantial amount of memory. The proposed BasicVSR++ method addresses this concern by refining these components to significantly reduce the computational load while maintaining exceptional performance. The new strategies include using fewer and more representative reference frames in a video for propagation and employing scale-aware feature alignment, which yields better results and mitigates complex motion issues. The enhanced BasicVSR method exhibits improved code complexity and is compatible with various GPU architectures, enabling fast and efficient code optimization. As a result, the method achieves exceptional performance in various evaluation metrics while demonstrating impressive generalization capabilities. The association with the MMAR2021 workshop allows the proposed method to be entered in recent video SR benchmarking challenges.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared knowledge across tasks can lead to destructive interference, causing learned policies to struggle and even result in random or uniform actions. By breaking down this shared knowledge into modular components and utilizing local information, such as the task name, we demonstrate the ability to implement stable multi-task reinforcement learning. Through both theoretical and empirical analyses, we find that model-based methods using this modular approach can achieve high performance, surpassing state-of-the-art results in comparison to both model-free and reward-sharing methods. Additionally, our proposed system mirrors the structure of the brain's cerebellum, consisting of layered modules that process input and output data, and we show that its efficiency and flexibility enable it to successfully learn complex non-linear tasks in a variety of environments.

Working in an ideal environment, we analyze the performance of classical heat engines when operating at finite powers. These theoretical engines are allowed to utilize only a limited number of control methods, resulting in a defined set of working fluids. As an example, we examine two specific scenarios, one where the engine's temperature is fixed and it interacts with a heat bath via a universal interface, and another where the engine's internal energy is defined by a polynomial function and it exchanges heat with a bath at two fixed temperatures. In both cases, we show that under restricted control, these engines reach a limit in their efficiency, which approaches the maximum possible efficiency as the number of available controls is increased. This efficiency gap is found to be a product of two factors: the engine's type and the extent of its thermal molecular interactions. In the case of thermal molecular interactions, this gap is shown to be constant, resulting from the interplay between the engine's internal degrees of freedom and the available controls. We derive a general formula for calculating the maximum efficiency in the 2-T scenario, and through our analysis, we verify that it reduces to the known universal formula under the condition of unlimited control.

This research proposes a methodology to assess the impact of hurricanes and storm surges on energy infrastructure. Existing methods for estimating repair costs and recovery times are inadequate, prompting the development of a dynamic modeling approach to analyze the spatial and temporal effects of storm-induced damage. By applying probabilistic principles to account for variable hurricane intensities and trajectories, the model can calculate distribution parameters for energy system performance metrics. By simulating 1000 sets of randomly generated hurricane scenarios, the model evaluates the performance of different energy system configurations. Results indicate a significant correlation between the number of damaged power transmission lines, storm severity, and recovery times. Furthermore, the model reveals that in high-risk areas with limited access to resources, underground facilities may experience prolonged service disruptions even if they are not physically damaged. Overall, the developed methodology provides a framework for conducting probabilistic assessments of energy system resilience against hurricane-driven disruptions and damage.

In this study, we established an extension of the three spheres theorem for monogenic functions under Clifford analysis framework. The theorem's proof is achieved by applying the unique tangent sphere theorem in a functional-analytic context. Building upon this result, we derived an essential extension of the three spheres theorem for Dirac eigenfunctions in n+1-dimensional space. Additionally, we discussed the implications of this result for eigenfunctions of elliptic operators and its connections to general linear differential equations.

Dyck systems serve as the simplest examples of non-positive entropy systems, consisting of a pair of maps that fulfill specific flow requirements on the positive entropy boundary. The entropy dynamics of these systems are difficult to understand directly. Positive entropy measures from these systems are difficult to converge to in an approachable manner. The entropy dynamics of these systems are explored through the analysis of a simplified model that can be graphically represented by the generalized baker map. The success of entropy approachability in the simplified model is hindered by two distinct failures: the first arises from the existence of too many non Approachable measures and the second from the fact that some non Approachable measures are not uniquely determined. These failures are more pronounced in the original Dyck system due to an infinite number of non Approachable measures with unclear unique determination status. The generalized baker map scenario shares characteristics with the success and failure mechanisms of the Dyck system.
